Preface

carly1990s.Elcctronic tradinghas transformed the markets,making thcm more accessiblc
than ever beforc.Tools like Direct Market Access (DMA)and algorithmic trading give
invcstors a lot morc control over how their strategics are executed. For instance, DMA
enables investors to send orders to exchanges, using their broker's infrastructure.
Acccssibility is great, but good traders are a special breed; thcy have a lot of expcrience
and detailed markct knowledge.Algorithmic trading distils some of this knowledge into pre-
packagcd rule-sets,or algorithms.A computerised system is responsiblefor executing ordcrs
by strictly following thesc rules,offering an efficient alternative tomanual trading.
Inorder togetthcmaximumbenefitfromtcchnologieslikealgorithmic trading andDMA
it is vital to havc a thorough understanding of them.Hopefully,by rcading this book you
should cndupwithagoodfundamentalknowledge of both of these topics,aswell as trading
and markets in gencral.
Who should read this book?
Algorithmic trading encompasses trading, quantitative analysis and computer programming.
Hencc, this book is targctcd towards all three areas. It should serve as a good introduction for
any investors,traders,salespeople,analysts,quantitative analysts (quants), or softwarc
developcrswhoarenewtothisfield.
The aim is to take thercadcrfrom thegroundup,sovcry littleknowledgeof themarkets
or trading is assumed.There are also no requirements for any programming knowlcdge.We
will revicw trading algorithms in some detail, but tablcs and diagrams will be used to
illustrate thcir function rather than snippets of code.Similarly,whilst there is some
mathematics in this book,it is not a mathematical text,so formulas arc provided only where
relevant.Examplcs are uscd tokeep the math in context.Rcfcrences are given for those who
might want to find the actual proofs.
Another aim of this book is to try to help bridge some of the gaps bctween the practice of
trading and the theory.Aphenomenal amount ofrescarch hasbeen carried outinto trading
and markets.Digitisationhas mcant that huge amounts of data arc now availablefor study.
Thc fields of econophysics and “phynance” arc also busily applying advanced techniques
from physics to analyse the markets. Somc of these studies arc highly theoretical; however,
there is also a large amount of empirical rcsearch,based on data from the world's major
markets.Throughout thisbook there arc sectionsproviding reviews of relevant research and

A wide range offinancial assets may be tradcd on the world's markets.One of the most

Chapter 4 focuses on orders. Thcse may simply reprcscnt trade instructions, but there are a

Chapter 5 covcrs the various types of trading algorithm in more detail. They are classified
using three main types, namely impact-driven(e.g. Volume Weighted Average Price
(VWAP), cost-driven (e.g. implementation shortfall) and opportunistic (e.g. liquidity
sceking).For each algorithm,we examine their basic mechanism and discuss common
variations. To enablc comparison, a standard example order is used throughout. This,
combined with charts showing thc potential trading patterns, highlights the differences (and
similarities)hetwcenthevariousalgorithms.
Chapter 6 concentrates on the importance of transaction cost analysis. Costs have a
significantcffectoninvestmentreturns;therefore,bothpre andpost-trade analysis arevital.
An cxample trade is used to decompose the transaction costs into their key components, such
as market impact and timing risk. To put this in perspective, some comparisons of costs
across the world's markcts are provided.
Chapter 7gocs on to considcr how the optimal trading strategymigh1 bc sclectcd.A
frameworkfor trading dccisionsis examincd;this assesscs ordersin terms of their difficulty.
Thc impact of invcstmcnt decisions/rcquiremcnts, such as benchmarks or risk avcrsion,is
also considercd. The “trader's dilemma” of balancing the trade-off bctween cost and risk is
visualised using the efficient trading frontier.This is then applied to the selection of trading
algorithms. The effect of both requirements and asset-specific factors, such as liquidity and
volatility,are then reviewed.A potential decision tree for algorithm selection is then
proposed.

1.3Coreexecutionmethods
Institutional trading can broadly be classificd as either agency or principal trading. In agency
trading, the broker acts as a conduit to the market, as we saw in Figure 1-1. The client may
also give trading instructions, such as to execute throughout the day or targct a specific
benchmark price or a certain percentage of the market volume.With principal trading, the
broker/dcaler agrees an up-front price for the asset, which they will fulfil either from their
owninventory or by executing on the markets.Since principal trading is carried out with a
specific dcaler, rather than at an exchange, this is also referred to as “over-the-counter
(OTC) trading.
In terms of risk, the client is exposed to the market with agency trading. The price may
move favourably (or not), there is also the possibility that the order may fail tobe completed.
The broker will strive to achieve best execution for the client, but at the end of the day they
are aeting as an agcnt for the client, they do not take on any of the risk.In comparison,with
principal trades the risk is transferred immediately to the broker/dealer. Consequently,
principal tradingis more expensive because the dealer tries to offset this by incorporating it
in the negotiated price. The investor must dccide whether the up-front costs are worthwhile
compared to thepotentialmarketrisk.
In general, both types of trading are supported for most equities and for the standardised

2.4 Trading mechanism research
The trading process can be broken down into threekey stagcs:
1.Pricc formation
2. Price discovery / trade execution
3.Reporting,clearing& settlement
In other words,we first need to decide on the price we are willing to trade at,referred to
as pricc formation. Secondly, for a trade to occur we need to find a countcrparty that is
prepared to trade with us at this price, also termed pricc discovery or trade execution.
Finally, the trades are reported and the clearing and settlement processes handle the requircd
cashflows and transfersof ownership.
Most research has focussed on thc first two phases,trying to determine the relationships
betwecn market structure,tradingvolumc,priccs and trading costs.
Price formation
Investors tend tohave differcntviews on the futurevalue of an asset;inpart,this isbecause
theyhavevarying levels of information.Consequently,their valuations targct diversc prices.
Therefore,price formation for an asset is usually based on supply and demand conditions.It
is also affected by the fundamental market mechanism, i.e. quote-driven or order-driven.
Marketmicrostructureresearchershaveuscdawiderangeofmodelstoinvestigatethis
proccss;Chapter8providesa more detailedreviewof these.
Quote-drivenmarkets are aperfectstartingpointfor analysisintopriceformation since
the very nature of markct makers is to quote prices. Information-based models assume that
some participants have a definiteinformation advantage over others.The bid offer spread
represents the cost for which markct makers arc prepared to trade. Essentially, this spread
shouldgenerateenoughreturnstocover thcircostsandanylossesfromtradingwithmore
informed traders. Inventory-based models derive the dealer's quote based on their inventory
(or position). This just needs to be sufficient to service any incoming orders. So the market
makcr's bid offer spread often tends to incrcasc as their position moves further from their
idealinvcntory.
For order-drivenmarkets,price formation is more complex since there are many more
participants, each with their own opinion. Order-driven markets are generally based around a
centrallimit orderbook,whichcontainseverylive orderfortheasset.Thescreenshotshown

illustratecachof theunderlyingorders(inthiscaseS6andS8)whichmakeupthesctotals.

Reporting, clearing and settlement
The final stages of the trading mechanism are reporting, clearing and scttlcment. Oncc a
trade has been exccuted, detailed confirmations of the deal must bc rcported to thc associated
counterparties,themarket authoritiesmay alsoneed tobe informcd.
The nex1 stage of the process is clearing, which is basically a preparatory step beforc
actual settlement. Clearing involves validating the trade and settlement details, as well as
ensuring that the buyer and seller have the requircd assets/funds to he able to proceed. Often,

## Page 67

AlgorithmicTrading&DMA
47
a spccific clearing agcnt will be mandated for trades at regulated venues such as cxchanges.
The settlerment process represents the actual exchange of assets and funds. The details for
the buycr and sellcr are matched; a payment is made from the buyer's account and the asset's
ownershipisreassigned.Nowadays,mostfinancial assets aredematerialised,sothisliterally
means updating a book cntry to reflect the change in ownership.However,for some assets,
such as commodities, it can still involve a physical delivery. Generally, this process is
handlcd by sccurity depositorics or dedicated custodians,financial institutions that specialise
in the safekeeping of asscts. Custodians also manage any associated interest or dividend
paymcnts, and even handle corporate actions for the holdings. Many security depositories
andcustodianshavenowbecomcintcrnational,cateringforawiderangeofmarketsand
allowingcrossbordertrading.
The clearing and settlement process has become incrcasingly automated to kecp up with
elcctronic trading. Straight-through-processing (STP) offers the prospect of a fully electronic
trading,clcaring and settlement pathway.Gradually,more and more markets are migrating to
support electronic clearing and settlement. Settlement dates used to commonly be five
working days aflter the actual execution,denoted as T+5.This is gradually shifting to T+1,
andultimatclytowardsT+O.
Increasingly, execution venues are adopting a central counterparty (CCP) approach for
their clearing and settlement. This effectively splits cach deal into two parts; cach half is then
transacted versus the CCP. So the huycr actually pays the CCP in return for the asset, whilst
the seller must dcliver the asset to the CCP in return for paymcnt. This helps reducc
countcrparly risk as well, since the central counterparty now bears the risk of default.The
CCP mcchanism also allows for fully anonymous trading,since each party will only need to
dcalwiththeCCP.Thcbuyer andsellerjustnccdtoprovidesufficientcollateral tocover
their tradcs. This also means clcaring can be netted across all a participant's trades for an
asset,rcsulting in a single net trade vcrsus the CCP. Clearly,such netting means much less
transfers and settlements and so can lead to substantial cost savings.It can also helpreduce
thc rcquircd margin(or collateral) commitmcnts needed to cover credit risk.Many central
countcrparties support margining across different asscts,so the margin for a futures position
maybereduced by a corrcspondingholdingin the underlyingassct.This can helpreduce thc
costsoffunding/positionmanagement.
For morc information on the clearing and settlement proccsses, the review by Marco
PaganoandJorgePadilla(2005)isagoodstartingpoint.
2.5Transaction cost measurement and analysis
Transaction costs are the last kcy arca for market microstructure research. Thcy are
unavoidable, and are incurred cach time an asset is bought or sold. Costs can have a

periods, helping to rcduce trading volumes and so decreasing overall markct liquidity.
Electronic tradinghashelpedincreasemarketaccess toawiderrangeofparticipants.In so
doing,it hasimprovedmarket efficicncyandled toa reductioninoverall transactioncosts.
By carcfully measuring and analysing transaction costs,we can try to minimise them.
Hence understanding how and why they occur has become a key factor in achieving
significant invcstmcnt returns. Clearly,the first stage is accurately measuring the overall
costs. Post-trade analysis has also proved important for performance analysis, enabling

andwhen an orderis dispatched.
Market impact: This represents how much effect the order has on the asset's price. Larger
orders result in a larger impact compared to smailer ones; however, the effect decreases
significantly with assct liquidity.Marketimpact consists of botha temporary effect and a
permanent one.The tcmporary market impact reflects the overall cost incurred by
demanding immediacy (when combined with the spread cost). Whercas the permancnt
impact signifies the long-term information cost of the trade, based on how it affects the
asset'soverallordcrbuy/sell imbalance.
Price trend: Asset prices may sometimes cxhibit broadly consistent trends.An upward
trend implies that costs will increase when buying an asset, whilst savings will be accrued if
selling,whcreas theopposite is truefor a downwardprice trend.
Timing risk:This cost reflects uncertainty,in particular for volatility in both the asset's
price and its liquidity. The more volatile an asset then the more likely its price will move
away and so incrcase the transaction costs. Similarly, if liquidity suddenly falls then market
impact costs will rise. Timing risk may be considerable, especially for volatile assets and for
ordersthathavealongtradinghorizon.
Opportunity cost:Orders are not always fully completed,maybe due topassive trading or
unfavourable market conditions. This cost represents the missed opportunity, since the next
day prices may move cven further away.

2.6Summary
Market microstructure concentrates onthe actual trading process,analysing howspecific
dcsigns or mechanisms affect both observed prices and traded volumes as well as
helping to cxplain the associated costs.

## Page 72

52
Market microstructure
Liquidity represents the cost for converting an asset into cash orvice versa.
Markcts may be classified in terms of two main mechanisms:
Purcly quote-driven markets,whcrc traders must transact with a dealer (or markct
maker), who quotes prices at which they will buy and sell a given quantity.
Purely ordcr-driven markets, where tradcrs participate equally,by placing ordcrs.
These are then matched on the order book using a consistent set of rules.
Increasinglymarkets are actuallyhybrids of thesc two approaches.
Trading maybe broken down into three main stages:
Priceformation
Price discovcry / trade exccution
Reporting,clcaring& settlement
Thcre are threekey mcthodsfortradecxecution:
Bilateral trading, which is a one-to-one negotiation often with a market maker.
Continuous auctions, where matching rules are applied each time an order is addcd,
updated or cancelled to determine whether there is a resultant cxccution.
Call auetions, where orders are allowed to accumulate for a set time before the
matehing rules are applied, and so hclping to reduce price volatility.
Transaction costs are unavoidable,they are ineurred each time an asset is bought orsold.
Cost measurement has focussed predominantly on spreads and bcnchmark prices. Costs
maybehrokendownintotwomainclasscs:
Explicit costs,sueh as commissions, fees and taxes,are clcarly identifiable and
easily measured.
Implicit costs, such as market impact and timing risk, are generally associatcd with
the actual trading process and are harder to identify and measure.

Financial assets generally provide their issuers with a means of financing themselves, and

Equity
Stocks allow companies to finance themselves by actually making their ownership public;
cach share represcnts a portion of the firm's inherent value,or equity. Thisvalue represents
what the corporation's remainingassets are worth once all the liabilities havebeen deducted.
A finite number of shares are issued by public corporations, although they may also choose
toissue new ones orbuybacksome of the outstanding shares.Firms may alsomakeperiodic
dividendpaymentstoshareholders.
Shares are forward looking investments,since theyrepresent a portion of thefirm’s total
equity.Investors cxpect the value of their shares to increase or dividends to be paid in order
to compensate themfor theriskofbankruptcy.
Determining the fairvaluefor equitiesisnon-trivial.Prescntvalue theory states that the
value of an asset corresponds to a discounted sum of its future payments. This may be based
on the present value of their future dividend payments. In turn, this depends on future
earnings,which canbe difficult to predict.Firms may also choose to reinvest some of their
income rather than increasing dividend payouts. Consequently, there are countless different
valuation methods that may be applied to companies, each trying to tackle the range of
possibilities.

Transparency
Transparency plays an important part in improving execution quality. lt is also a key factor
in reflectingthe accessibilityofmarkets.Pre-andpost-tradeinformationisvitalfor effectivc
trading.Venucsneedtoprovidetimelydata on the size andprice oforders/quotes/trades,as
well as the time of executions.Historically,quote-driven or OTC markets have tended to be
muchlesstransparent thanorder-drivcnones.
Post-trade transparency is well established for cxchange-based markets. But it is also
improving for OTC markets.For instance,in the U.S., the Trade Reporting and Compliance
Engine (TRACE) initiative has mandatcd reporting of trade prices for corporate debt since
2001. This may well expand to includc primary market, government agency and debt from
the Federal National Mortgage Association (Fannie Mae) and Federal Home Loan Mortgage
Corporation (Freddie Mac). In Europe, MiFID has mandated reporting for OTC equity
trades. This may also spread to encompass other European asset classes, such as bonds and
OTCderivatives.
Pre-trade transparency poscs more issues, since for OTC markets only the broker/dealers'
bestbid and offer are availablc.Multi-broker platforms/markets improve this slightly by
making it easier to discover and to compare quotes from a range of market makers. In
comparison, exchangcs and othcr cxecution venues based on electronic order books are
capablc of much morc transparency. They may allow the best five bids and offers or even the
cntire orderbooktohcviewed.
Convcrscly,there is also aglobal trend formore prc-trade anonymity.Whilst transparcncy
is important toscc thc currently available prices andliquidity,it can also pose problcms for
participants who nced to trade larger quantities. Signalling risk represents the information
that may begivcn away by suchlarge orders.Pre-trade anonymity helps reduce the
signallingrisk,as can the adoption of order splittingoralgorithmicstrategies.Anonymity is
generally only offered by ordcr-driven venues and a few multi-broker platforms. This is
bccause prime-brokerage type agreements and ccntral counterparties are available, which
help to reduce the potential credit and settlement risk. So for most OTC trading the only
clientprotectionisstill thetwo-wayquote.
A justification for these seemingly opposing trends in transparcncy and anonymityis
providcd by Robert Schwartz and Michael Pagano (2005). They point out that whilst
transparcncy is requircd for price discovery, opacity is required for quantity discovery. This
cxplains the popularity of “dark pool" ATSs which allow participants to anonymously trade
in size. Ironically, some of the succcss of the “dark pools" is due to the transparency of the
primary exchanges. Since, in general, they match based on size, using prices discovered from
the primary exchangc. Thus, dark pools have so far been concentrated in markets where
priccs are readily available, such as the equities markets. They are also starting to be
introduccd for the FX and listed derivatives markcts.Negotiation based“dark pools"could
be cstablished for other asset classes, albeit with the additional burden of price discovery.

4.1 Introduction
Orders reprcsent execution instructions. They allow investors and traders to communicate
their rcquircments, both from thc type of order chosen as well as with a range of additional
conditions and directions. This chapter focuses on thc basic mechanics of these various order
types and conditions.
The two main order types arc market orders and limit orders.In terms of liquidity
provision, thcsc are complete opposites. Market orders demand liquidity; they require
immediatc trading at the bcst price available. Whereas limit orders provide liquidity, they act
as standing orders with inbuilt price limits, which must not be breached (a maximum price
for buys and a minimum price for sclls).
The conditions thatmaybc applied to each ordcr allow the traderto control manyfeatures
of thc exccution, for example:
Bothhow andwhcnitbecomes active
Its lifetime/duration
Whcther it may bc partially filled
Whcthcritshouldberoutcdtoothervenuesorlinkcd tootherorders
A widc range of trading styles can be achieved just by combining thcsc conditions with
limit and market orders. Indecd, many venues have gone on to support an even broadcr
spcctrum of orders, all essentially derived from basic market and limit orders. These include:
·Hybrid orders, such as market-to-limit
Conditional orders,such as stops and trailingstops
·
Hiddcn and iceberg orders
Discretional orders, such as peggcd orders
Routed ordcrs,such as pass-through orders
New order typcs are continuing to evolve. Some venues evcn offer orders that bchave like

volumc. Indccd,the line bctwccn them and trading algorithms is bccoming increasingly
blurred. Dynamic order typcs arc very similar to trading algorithms, since they both alter

orders generally only focus on one specific variable, often the current market pricc (c.g. stop

Auction/Crossing session instructions
Auction/session instructions are used to mark an order for participation in a specific auction,

Venucs with intraday auctions generally support an intraday auction or a “next auction"

The all-or-none (AON) instruction enforces a 100% completion requirement on an order.
Unlike the fill-or-kill instruction there is no requirement for immediacy, so all-or-none
orders may pcrsist for some time. This can pose a problem for order book based systems,

price of an AON sell, particularly if the AON order is large. Thus, AON orders are given a
lowerpriorityfor execution,and are oftenhandledby storing them on a separate conditional
order book. This additional complexity has meant that many of the markets which once

usingIOC orfill-or-kill orders instead.

Preferencing and directed instructions
Order prefercncing and directed instructions pcrmit bilateral trading, since thcy direct ordcrs

Note that NASDAQ uscd to offer directed orders viaSelcctNct,but retired thisin 2005.
Directed non-liability orders allowed the market makcr five seconds to accept,partially
accept,decline orissuc a counter offerfor the order.NowwhenNASDAQrefcrs todircctcd

Exccution venucs have often catered for additional routing instructions for orders. Thus
providing agateway scrvice that allows orders tobe routcd to other venues aswell as
handling them locally.
In the U.S. equities markct, the introduction of Regulation-NMS has made routing

So if an order might “trade-through” the best price available at another venue, the host venue

Do-not-route
This instruction ensures that the executionvenue will handle the order locally and not route

no-prefercnce orders on NYSEArca.

Directed-routing

Linking Instructions
Linking instruetions provide a means of introdueing dependeneies between orders.
A one-canecls-other (OCO) instruetion may be used to make two orders mutually
exclusive, often this is used to close out of a position. For instance, to capitalise from any
gains on a long position we could place a sell order at a high price. If the market moves
against us, it makes sense to also have a separate stop order at a lower price. Clearly, we do
not want both orders to execute since this would not only flatten our position but could
actually reverse it,leading to a short position.By linking the two sells with an OCO
instruction, we can ensure that if either of the sell orders cxecutes then the other will
immcdiatelybe cancelled.Note that if one of the OCO orders is cancellcd the other remains
unaffected.
A One-triggers-other (OTO) instruction links a supplementary order that will only be
created upon the suecessful execution of the main order. For example, a successful buy order
could automatically spawn a stop order as proteetion from any losses.The secondary order is
contingent on themain order,andsois sometimes referred to as anif-done order.Note that if
the primary ordcr is cancelled then the secondary order will also he cancelled;however,this
linkage docs not work the otherway around.
Some venues even allow orders to be grouped. For example, the SAXESS trading
platform supportsbothlinked and combination orders.Linked orders effectivelyprovide an
"OR" logie, so for a given amount we can buy assets ABC, DEF or XYZ.As an order fills
for one asset, the other orders all reduce their sizes proportionally. Combination orders
provide “AND" logic linking both the prices and sizes for two distinet orders, effeetively
allowing spread trading.We shall go through these order-contingent types in more detail in
seetion 4.5.
Miscellaneousinstructions
So far,we have foeussed on the instructions that are commonly adopted across most

what additional instruetions are supported. Some of the more common miscellaneous
instructions are:
Identity details:Many venues offer anonymity by default.Although somc others still

Short-sales: This flag must be set for markets that enforce short sales regulations. This is
used to enforce tick-sensitive trading, i.e. selling only on an uptiek or even tick.
Odd-lots: Some venues incorporate odd-lot trading together with thc normal trading
mechanism. This instruetion allows round lot orders to be matehed with odd-lots.
Settlement instructions:Generally,non-standard settlement instructions require
negotiation,and depcnding on the conditions mayineurhigherbroker fecs or maynot even
he possible. However, some rcasonably common non-standard instructions are supported,
such as foreign curreney settlement. Cash settlement is the most common alternative for

Hybrid order types
In many ways, market orders and limit orders represent different ends of the spcctrum.

Market-to-limitorders
Market-to-limit orders are indecd a hybrid: a market order with a strong implicit price limit.
Whentheorderfirstarrives,itbehaveslikeamarketorder,seekingliquidityat thehest

price it will convert into a standing limit order for the residual amount.
For example, if we issue a market-to-limit order to buy 2,000 ABC, as shown in Figure
4-12, the initial market order will immediately cross with the order S1. This price now

fill of 1,000 at 101 is achieved and the order now converts to a limit order at this last
executed price, as shown in Figure 4-12(c) as order B4.

theirvaliditybycomparing thecurrentbeslpriccwiththe last tradedpricc.

Stops are somctimcs also referred to as stop-loss ordcrs. Since as sells (buys) they are
gcnerally used as a safcty net to protect profits, by closing out long (short) positions should
the market move against us, as we can sce in Figure 4-14. So, for example, let's assume a
long position was initiated at 92; once the price rcaches 93 a stop sell order is placed (at 93)
as protection. If thc price trcnd reverts at timc t, as shown in pathway (a),thcn the stop will
be triggered. Altcrnativcly, if the price continues to trend favourably (b) the stop will remain
inactive.
Note that the markct order generated by a stop gives no guarantees on the price achieved.
T'his is important sincc the very nature of stops means that they are only activated when the
markct price becomes unfavourable.They offer the lesser of two evils; a poor price may be
achicved,butif themarket doesnotrevert,the alternativeis evenworse.
Stoplimit orders replace the markct order with a limit order.The stop pricc activates the
order,whilst the limit price controls the triggered order.Although this offers some price
protectionby controlling the price of the triggered order,it alsointroduces ariskoffailing to
cxecutc.Unfortunately,fastmarket conditions often heighten thisrisk.
The market-with-protection order type acts as a halfway house betwecn market orders and
a limit orders. Stop orders with protection use this order type to increase the probability of
execution whilst still having a limit for some price control.The limit priceis based on the
stop price and the specificd protcetion limit. Nevertheless, it is still fundamentally a limit
ordcr,so if thc price shifts are severe enough to breach the protcction limit then the position
will remain exposed.
Therefore,if closing out of a position is a must then thcrc is no real choicc other than by
using a purc stop order. lt may also be worth considering other means of hedging the
position,such aswith options or futures.
Whilst stop orders arc a useful tool, thcy can also havc considerable market impact,in
particular when thc market is at its most vulnerable. Upon activation, all stop ordcrs tcnd to
acceleratc the pricc trend that triggered them. For instance, a sell stop order is trying to scll
when there has alrcady been a significant fall in thc price. Such a drop is most likely due to
animbalance bctwcen the orderbookvolume tobuy andsell.Thestop orderis effectively
looking for liquidity when it has already decreased.If it manages to executc then the
imbalanccwillbcevengrcaler.

Contingent/if-touchedorders
Contingcnt,orif-touched,orders are effectively the opposite of stops.For foreign exchange,
they are sometimes called entry ordcrs since thcy are gencrally used to cstablish positions.
As with stops, there are two main types, a market if-touched ordcr and a limit if-touched.
Note that alimit if-touchcd orderis similar to a standinglimit order,cxcept thatis hidden
fromtheorderbookuntilactivated.
Their operation is extremely similar to stops;both remain hidden until the market pricc
moves sufficiently to activate them, whereupon they create a corresponding order. But the
activation logic is the reverse of that for stops. So a buy if-touchcd order is triggered when
the market price hits the target price or moves bclow, whilst a scll triggcrs when thc market
price hits the target or movcs above.
Some venucs cven allow if-touched orders that are contingent on the price of a completely
diflerentasset,such asastockindex.
Ticksensitiveorders
Tick-scnsitive instructions introduce a validity conditionbased on thelast traded price.If thc
current price is the same as the last trade it is referrcd to as a zero tick, above it is an up tick
and below is a downtick. (Note zero ticks may be further classified as zcro up and downticks
bycomparingwiththelastdifferenttradeprice).
Thus,a buy downtick order may onlybe crossed on a downtick or zero downtick pricc.
Likewise, a sell up tick order may only be crossed on an up tick or a zero uptick. Larry
Harris (1999)points out that tick sensitivc orders are essentially limit ordcrs with
dynamically adjusting limit prices.Tick sensitive orders employ a similar pricclatching
mechanism to trailing stops; a downtick order will raise its dynamic limit price only whcn
thepriceincreases,whilst anuptickorderwill onlydecrcaseitslimitwhenthepricefalls.
Tick sensitivc orders have no immediate market impact. The tick dependency mcans that
immediacy is sacrificed in order to obtain a price one tickbetter.Harris observes that they
are thereforemostusefulwhenthe ticksize islarge.Infact,thedecimalisation of theU.S.
stockmarketsin2000 actuallyreduccd the appcalof tick dependcncy,sinceit meant thatfor
most stocks the ticksize decreascdfrom a sixteenth tojustIcent.
Tick dependent orders exist mainly because of regulation, in part to try to curh thc
downward price momentum due to hidden stop orders being triggcred. Conscqucntly, some
venues enforce a rule that short sales must be on an uptick. In other words, an uncovcred salc
is only allowed when the current price is above the last traded price.

Iceberg/reserveorders
As its name suggests, an iceberg order comprises of a small visible peak and a significantly
larger hidden volume.The peak (or display) size is configurable,although some venues
stipulate a minimum, often a percentage of the normal market sizc (NMS). The visible
portion of the order is indistinguishable from any other limit order. Each time this displayed
order is fully executed the venue's trading system splits a new order from the hidden
volume, until the whole iceberg order is completed. Therefore, each displayed order has
normal time priority within the order book whilst the hidden volume just has price priority.

4.6Summary
Orders are the fundamental building block for any trading strategy.
Orders represent execution instructions. There are two main types:
Market orders buy or sell a given quantity at the best price possible. They focus on
completing the order with no specific price limit, and so demand liquidity.
Limit orders buy or sell a given quantity at a specified price or better. The price
limit must not be breached, even at the risk of failing to execute. They persist until
executed or cancelled and so provide liquidity.

## Page 133

AlgorithmicTrading&DMA
113
A range of optional conditions allow control over factors such as:
How andwhen the orderbecomes active.
Its lifetime/duration.
Whether it maybe partiallyfilled.
一
Participationinauction/crossingsessions.
一
Whether it should be directed to specific venues orevenmarket makers.
一
Linking with other orders.
Miscellaneousfactors,such as odd lots and settlement handling.
More specialised order types(derived from both market and limit orders) offer:
Hybrid orders, such as market-to-limit, which try to offer the best of both limit and
marketorders.
Conditional orders,such asstops,whichbasetheirvalidityonasetcondition.Only
when the condition is met will it result in an actual order being placed.
Hidden orders try to reduce signalling riskfor large orders.
一
Discretional ordersoffermoredynamichandlingof limit prices.
一
Routed orders allow more complex routing logic than possible via conditions.
Order-contingent orders,whichoffermorecomplexlinkingrelationships.
New order types are continuing to evolve. Some venues even offer orders that behave
like algorithms,such as targeting theVWAP or participating in a set percentage of the
market volume. Indeed, the line between them and trading algorithms is becoming
increasinglyblurred.

5.1 Introduction
An algorithm is basically a set of instructions for accomplishing a given task. Thcrefore, a
trading algorithm simply defincs thc steps required to cxccutc an order in a specific way.
Brokcrs/vendors provide a rangc of trading algorithms,each with distinct goals.Some strive
tomatch or beat a spccific benchmark,or try to minimise overall transaction costs whilst
othcrs seek to trade more opportunistically.To achieve thcsc goals,some approaches rigidly
adherc toagiven trading schedulewhilst others aremore dynamic,adapting toever-
changing market conditions.
Although the individual rules may be quite straightforward, the wide array of different
events and possibilities that must be catcred for mean algorithms can rapidly becomc quite
complex. A common way of tackling this complexity has been to split the problem in two.
For instance,Vladimir Kazakov (2003) decomposes VWAP trading into determining the
optimum trading strategy and then realising this with optimal execution. The strategy
concentratcs on the trading schedule and benchmark, whilst the execution focuses on
choosing appropriate orders to achicvc this. Similarly, Robert Kissell and Roberto Malamut
(2005) propose brcaking algorithmic trading down into macro and micro level decisions.
Again,the macro levcl makes strategic choices,based on the overall objectives.The micro
level considers more tactical dctails,such as the spccifics of order submission.
As an example,let's takc a simple order to buy 6,000 of asset ABC over the next hour and
time-slice its cxecution so that we trade 1,0o0 every ten minutes. We can represent this task

5.2Categorising algorithms
Although there arc a wide variety of trading algorithms out thcre,if we strip off the
customisations, we can start to see a small sct of core strategies that are commonly providcd

One way of classifying thcse algorithms is based on thc benchmarks that they use. For

VWAPit is dynamic,andMarkct-on-Closcsecks tomatch a future closing pricc.
Another way of classifying algorithms is based on thcir fundamental mechanisms. Ian
Domowitz and HenryYegerman(2005a) describe these as a continuum,which ranges from
unstructured strategies, such as liquidity seeking algorithms, to highly structured approaches,
such as a VWAP algorithm. Jian Yang and Brett Jiu (2006) go on to extend this approach by
splitting this continuum into thrce main calegories, namely:
·Schedule-driven
·Evaluative
Opportunistic
Purely schedule-driven algorithms follow a strictly dcfincd trading trajectory, gcncrally
created statically from historical data. For instance, historical volume profilcs have often
been uscd to implement VWAP algorithms; they represent intra-day historical volume
averages. Thcsc profiles may then be used as a template for how the ordcr should bc split
overtime.
At the other cnd of thc spectrum, opportunistic algorithms are complctely dynamic. They
react to favourable market conditions, trading more aggrcssivcly to take advantage of thcm.
Then as conditions become less favourable, they trade more passively, if at all. Hence,
liquidity-seeking algorithms are a good fit for this category.
Evaluative algorithms represent the middlc ground between these two extremes. Oftcn
thcy combine aspects of each approach.Indeed,Yang and Jiu (2006) suggcst that at thc
macroleveltheymaybehaveinamorcschedule-drivenfashionwhilstatthemicro-level
they focus on balancing the trade-off between cost and risk. Algorithms targeling
implementationshortfall aregoodfitforthe evaluativecategory.

Percent of Volume (Pov)
Percent of volume (POV) algorithms “go along” with the market volume; hence, they are
also sometimcs called volume inline,participation, target volume or follow algorithms.

BasicMechanism
Unlike algorithms, such as TWAP and VWAP,whcre a trading schedule may be

algorithm tries to participate in the markct at a given rate, in proportion with the market

Another way of looking at price adaptive strategies is based on how they handle overall
price trends. An AIM stratcgy assumes that trends are short-lived and will soon revert,
whereas a PIM approach relies on the trend persisting. Thus, AIM trading will immediately
try to take advantage of any favourable prices, and hope that unfavourable prices will revert.
Conversely,PIM trading will react aggressively to stem any potential losses from an
unfavourable trend,but it will bepassive duringfavourable trends,hoping to achievefurther
price improvement.
BasicMechanism
Essentially, this is still an implementation shortfall algorithm, so the basic behaviour will
follow an IS approach. But in addition, the algorithm dynamically adapts to market
conditions. Effectivcly, this is like having a tilt function that adjusts in real-time based on the
currentmarketconditions.
Initially, a bascline target for volume partieipation may be determined, based on the
cstimated optimal trade horizon.During trading,the adaptive portionis then used to modify
this rate. The results for an example trade to buy 10,000 ABC using both AIM and PIM
approaches is shown inFigure5-17.

Market Close (MC)
Thc closc price is often used for marking to market, and calculating net asset values and

Basic Mechanism
Clcarly,the main issuc for a markct close algorithm is the fact that the benchmark is

causesignificantmarketimpact.
Manymarket closc algorithms determine an optimaltradinghorizonusingquantitative

can calculate an optimal start time, as Middleton (2005) points out.Figure 5-20 shows thc

5.6 Opportunistic algorithms
Opportunistic algorithmshave evolved from a range of trading strategies.They all take
advantage of favourable market conditions, whether this is based on pricc, liquidity or
anotherfactor.
Pricc inlinc algorithms arc essentially bascd on an underlying impact-driven strategy such
as VWAP or POV. What they add is price sensitivity, which enables them to modify their
trading style based on whcther the current market price is favourable or not. So a focus on
markct impact has given way to a more opportunistic approach.
Similarly, liquidity-driven algorithms are an evolution of simpler rule-based order routing
strategies. The trading is driven by the available liquidity, although cost is also a factor.
Whilst pair trading is effcctively a markct neutral strategy, so risk is less of a conccrn.
Instcad,thekey driver is whcn the spread orratiobetween the assets is favourable.
Notc that foreach of these algorithmsprice is still an importantfactor.Target benchmarks
provide a baselinc that allows them to gaugc whether the market conditions are favourablc or
not. Since thcy are so dynamic, opportunistic algorithms tend to be much more closely
aligncd totheirunderlying execution tactics than other algorithms,aswewill seeinChaptcr
9.In the following scctions,we shall examinc each of the opportunistic algorithms in somc
moredcpth.

Liquidity-driven
Liquidity represents the ease of trading a specific asset, so it has a considcrable effect on
overall transaction costs. Highly liquid assets tend to trade in greater volume, and so often
will have lower spreads and more depth available.Whereas for illiquid assets,activity is
much lower, the spread higher and order book may have little visible depth. So finding
liquidity is an important means of reducing costs, particularly for illiquid asscts.
Originally, liquidity-based trading simply mcant making decisions based on thc availahle
order book depth,rather than just the best bid and offer.In today's fragmentcd markets
liquidity-secking has become more complicated.For example, thc U.S.equity market has
dozcns ofpossible executionvenues,withthenumber continuing toincrease.In such an
environment, visualising the available liquidity becomcs non-trivial. If a trading strategy
focuses on just one execution vcnue, there is a danger that it will miss opportunities on the
other venues and so achieve a poorer execution price. Hence, for fragmented markcts
liquidity aggregation has hecome an important tool. Essentially, just as multi-brokcr systems
pooled dealer quotcs,we gather as much order book data as possible from evcry vcnuc and
aggregate these into a virtual ordcr book. Figure 5-25 shows an cxamplc that pools the orders
from thc primary exchange(Exch-1)and severalelectronic crossing networks (ECNs)and
“dark pool”alternative trading systems (ATSs).
Liquidity aggregation can bc as simplc as summing the available ordcrs at each price point
across all the different venues. For assets such as futurcs or options, this might also mcan
accounting for liquidity“implied”from more complex spread strategies.However, as we
saw in Chapter 4,venues are increasingly adopting implicd order typcs to make such
liquidity more easily available. Still, there are some further complications such as fccs and
latencics.Venueshave their ownfeestructures,so the algorithm needs toconsider thiswhen
comparing prices. Latency is also an issue, since any time lag between our orders being sent
andprocessed could significantlyreduce theprobability of exccution.
Given that execution is not guaranteed, it is also important to deal with execution
probability whcn choosing between venues. Notice that in Figure 5-25 thc timc field has
been replaced by a percentage. This represents the overall probability of cxecution for that
volumc.For order E1,on ECN-1,we estimate a 70% chancc of crossing with this order if we
now dispatched an order to sell at 10o.This perccntage is bascd on a rangc of factors,
including theprobability of cancellation,latency and historicalresults.

that price. Thus on ATS-1 order H3 corresponds to a 15% probability that this“dark pool"

Pair trading
Pair trading involves buying one asset whilst simultancously selling another. Therefore, this

sufficicntly correlated. The idcal situation is that thc asset we bought increascs in price,
whilst the one we sold falls.Although so long as the profit on one side of the trade outweighs
any loss on the other sidc,we should still come ou1 ahead.The profits may then be lockcd in

Multi-leg
Trading strategies for bonds, futures and options often involve multiple legs. Each leg
represents an order for a specifie asset. These might be as simple as a two-way spread trade,
although they may have three or four legs or be even more complex. However complex they
mightbe,these are stillusuallyrelativevalue trades,seeking to take advantage of differenees
in pricing hetween assets. Overall, they go long the currently under valued asset/s, hoping
that in the future the prices will rebalance netting us a profit. Essentially, they are much the
same as pairs (or sprcad) trading, although they may consist of baskets (or portfolios) of
trades.

GammaWeightedAveragePrice(GWAP)
lmplementation shortfall has become ubiquitous in the equitics markets, although there is
still a large contingent of traders and investors who also track benchmarks such as VWAP.
Still,VWAPisnotneccssarilya universalbenchmark,particularlyforfragmentedmarkets or
illiquidassets.TheGammaWeightedAveragePrice(GWAP)is analternativebenchmark
outlined by Scott Larison(2008).It is designed to tackle some of the shortcomings of VWAP
for the options markets: A single asset may have thousands of related options contracts, so
the liquidity of any one contract will generally be significantly lower than that of the
underlying asset. As Larison points out, this lower trading activity makes benchmarks like
VWAPlessmeaningfulfor options.Afurther complicationis thefactthat complexmulti-lcg
strategies represent a considerable volume in the options markets. Thus, prices may also be
influenced by those of other contracts.So the GWAPbenchmark also takes into account the
VWAP of the underlying asset.It maybe rcpresented as:

Gwap(put)= P-[△'*Aroc]
where P is the option price, 'is the adjusted delta and Aroc is the rate of change price. In
turn, the rate of change price (lroe) is based on the VWAP of the underlying asset:

whereSis thereferenceprice of the underlying asset,forexample,the arrivalprice orthe
previous close, and Svwap is the VWAP average for the specified interval.
The delta is one of the “Greeks"; it is a measure that represents the risk in terms of price
moves by the underlying asset. 4 A delta of 1.0 means that for every rise (fall) of $1 in the
underlying asset the option's price will also rise (fall) by $1. Conversely, a negative delta
means that the option's price moves in the opposite direction.In the GWAP calculation, the
adjusted delta (△) is bascd on the option's implied delta (△) and gamma (y) from when the
orderwasentered:
(call) =△+(roc *)′(put)=△-(roc*y)
Gamma is a second derivative risk measure. It quantifies how much the delta will change
when the underlying asset's price moves by one unit, e.g. $1. For example, let's consider a
call option priced at $6with a delta 0.5 and a gamma of 0.1.When the underlying asset price
increases by $1,the delta means the call option will increase to $6.5,whilst its delta will
increase to 0.6 because of the gamma.We shall cover both of these in more detail in Chapter
13inthereviewofdeltaandgammahedgingstrategies.

5.8Summary
A trading algorithm is simply a sct of instructions used to execute an order.
Trading algorithms may bc broadly categorised into thrcc main groups hased on the
target objectives. Thesc are impact-driven, cost-driven or opportunistic.
Impact-driven algorithms seek to minimise the overall market impact costs,usually by
splittinglarger ordcrs intosmaller child orders.
TWAP (time weighted average pricc) is often driven by a time-hased schedule.
VWAP (volume weighted average price) often uses historical volumes as a guide.
Perccnt of volume (POV) algorithms “go along”with the market volumc.
Minimal impact algorithms use ATSs and“dark pools”to rcduce signalling risk.
Cost-driven algorithms aim to reduce the overall trading costs.
Implemcntation shortfall (IS) sccks to achieve a balance between cost and risk.
Adaptive shortfall algorithms extend this, adapting to the market price (or liquidity).
Markct-on-close algorithmstargetthefutureclosingprice.
Opportunistic algorithms strive to takc best advantage of favourable market conditions.
Price inline algorithms are price-scnsitive variants of impact-driven algorithms.
Liquidity-driven algorithms are an evolution of simplcr rule-based ordcr routing.
Pairtradingis amarketncutral strategydrivenby afavourablesprcadorratio.
Most of these algorithms will work across asset classes. Still, the unique featurcs of
some asset elasses mean that completely new types may also be necded. For instancc:
Multi-legtradingforbondsandderivatives
Algorithms drivenbyfactorssuchasinterestratesorvolatility
Handling fungible assets, so specification-based trading rathcr than cxplicit asscts
Targeting new more appropriate benchmarks

6.1 Introduction
Each time an asset is bought or sold transaction costs are incurred. ln economic terms,
Robert Kissell (2006) describcs them as costs paid by buyers,but not received by the sellers.
They can have a considerable effect on investment returns, for instance,Ed Nicoll (2004)
estimatcd total annual transaction costs of approximately $120billion for the$12trillion
U.S. cquity markct. This is bascd on costs pcr order ranging from 20 basis points (bps) up to
200(or 2%)of thc valuc.Thewidc range is paruly due to the different characteristics of each
asset and ordcr,but is also due to the different ways transaction costs may be assigned.
Onc of thc most common ways to examine transaction costs has been to compare the
actual performancc of a portfolio with its “paper” equivalent. A papcr portfolio is simply a
virtual portfolio tradcd at benchmark prices, but without accounting for any costs.

Spreads
Spread cost represents the difference between the best bid and offer prices at any given time.
The spread compensates those who provide liquidity. Clearly, aggressive trading styles will
result in a higherspreadcost thanpassive ones.
The overall spread cost may be dctermined by summing the bid offer spreads for cach
cxccution. (A factor of 0.5 is used since we only pay half the sprcad for cach trade):
Spread Cost =∑(x;*(0.5* s))
where x, is the sizc of each execution and s, is the bid offer spread at that time.Note that
this is the quoted sprcad at the time of each execution, rather than the elfective spread, which
alsoincorporatestheimmediatemarketimpact.
In Example 6-1: Spread Cost =(10,000 * (91.1-91)) + (20,000*(92.4-92.2))
+ (15,000 * (93.45-93.4))
=$ 5,750
= 13 bps
Spread costs vary considerably across both markets and assets. For some asscts/markets,
the spread can be a major cost factor. In the U.S. equity market, decimalisation sharply
reducedspreadcosttoaround5bps,althoughduring the2007-09financialcrisis spreads
nearly doubled. In Europe and Japan spreads may be much higher, ranging from 10-50 bps
or even more. Unsurprisingly, large-cap and liquid stocks have lower spreads. More volatile
stocks tend tohavehighcrsprcads.
The simplcst way to lower spread costs is to trade more passively,using limit orders
which are priced at the markct or just behind it.Algorithms may not always directly consider
sprcad cost, although it may affect thcir choicc of cxccution tactics (passive or aggressive).
Most pricc-bascdexecution tactics willclosely monitor thc sprcadin ordcr to usc an
appropriate level of aggressionwhcnplacing and updating orders.
Marketimpact
Markct impact represents the price change caused by a specific trade or order. Generally,it
has an adverse affect, for instance, helping drive prices up when we are trying to buy.
The exact market impact cost is the difference hetween the actual price chart and thc
hypothetical one that would have occurred if our order had not becn crcated. Though, this
makcs market impact difficult to mcasure and estimate accurately, as Kissell and Glantz
(2003)obscrve.Figure6-7triestoshow thiscffectfortheorderfromExample6-1;thc
hypothetical price chart is labelled as the “paper” onc (borrowing from Perold's
implementation shortfall nomenclature).
Markct impact is usually broken down into tcmporary and permanent impacts:
Markct Impact=Temporary Impact+Permanent Impact
(6-3)
The temporary impact rcflects the cost of demanding liquidity. For instancc, an order that

Permanent impact corresponds to the long-term cffcct of our ordcr,rcprcsenting thc
information content that it has exposed to the market. Clearly, if the markct detccts a largc

large order might have a larger temporary impact than a serics of smallcr ordcrs. Howevcr,

Opportunity cost
Opportunity cost reflccts the cost of not fully executing an ordcr. This may be because the
asset's price went beyond a client's price limit or could just be due to insufficient liquidity.
Either way, it represents a missed opportunity, since the next day prices may move even
further away.
The ovcrall cost maybe determined as thc product of theremaining order size and the
price difference betwecn the final price (pv) and the arrival price:
OC=(x-∑x;)(PN- Po)
Unlike the othcr cost components,opportunity cost represents a virtual loss rather than a
physical one. Thc loss is only realised when a new order makes up the remainder at a lcss
favourableprice.
So for Examplc 6-1:Opportunity Cost =(50,000-45,000) *(93.0-90.65)
=$11,750
=26 bps
If thc price trcnd reverts tomorrow then it should be easy to purchase the remaining 5,000
XYZ at less than 93.0. 1f the trend continues then an opportunity cost of at least 26 bps will
be realiscd.

Determining how difficult an order will be depends on a range of propcrties.Wagner (2006)

momentum and urgcncy. Conversely, the key feature that makes trading easy is liquidity.

Ordersize:

closcly linked to the asset's liquidity. A large order for a highly liquid asset will tend to
causcmuchlessmarket impact thanfor an illiquid one.

Theefficienttradingfrontier
In Chaptcr 1,we saw the efficient frontier for portfolios proposed by Harry Markowitz
(1952). This plots the optimal portfolio in terms of returns for different levcls of risk (or
volatility). However, trading strategies are generally morc focussed on cost, so Robert
Almgrcn and Neil Chriss (2000) proposed thc efficicnt trading fronticr. They reasoned that
rational tradcrs would always seek to minimize expcctcd costs for a certain level of risk.
Hencc, an optimal trading strategy was defined as onc for which there were no alternatives
withlower expected costs for thc same dcgree of risk.The set of optimal solutions werc
termed the efficient trading frontier,consisting of a single solution for cvery possiblc level of
risk. In order to determine this frontier they sought to solve the following unconstrained
optimizationfortheexpectedcostE(x):

Morton Glantz proposed an approximation by fitting an exponential decay curve to just a few
specific strategies. More details may be found in Kissell and Glantz (2003).

Optimaltradingstrategies
VWAP:
The VWAP algorithm concentrates on minimizing market impact, by splitting the order
into quantities based on the historical volume profile.Although for smaller orders this may
unnecessarily prolong trading, causing additional risk exposurc.So, a VWAP order left to
trade through the whole dayhas one of thehighest associated risks.This maybe used as a
reference point on the efficient trading frontier,labelled as VWAP/day in Figure 7-10.
Simply by reducing the trading time to one appropriate for the order size, the risk may be
considerably reduced (labelled VWAP). Notice that the cost does not significantly increase
to achieve this.
TWAP:
In Figure 7-10, TWAP is shown as the only algorithm not to be actually on the efficicnt
trading frontier.This is because when a TWAP algorithm splits an order it does not take into
accountmarketconditions.Soitmayincuradditionalmarketimpactcomparedtoother
algorithms (except for small ordcrs or very liquid assets). Still, in terms of risk it is similar to
VWAP, either spread over the whole trading day or for a shortcr period. Thus, TWAP is
showndirectlyaboveVWAPontheefficienttradingfrontier.(Notethatforvenucswhere
volumeinformationisnotavailableTWAPisaviablealtcrnativetoVWAP.)
Percentofvolume(Pov):
POV algorithms have a similar goal to VWAP, namely minimization of market impact.
The only real difference bctween the two approaches is that the trading trajectory for a POV
algorithm isgenerated dynamically,basedon afixedproportion of the actual marketvolume.
Since its participation is based on the current market volume, each order is more likely to
complete in a timescale appropriate for its size. Consequently, the timing risk should be
reduced compared to VWAP, although the market impact cost may be slightly higher to
achieve this. So, on the efficient trading frontier, POV algorithms arc positioned to the just
left of VWAP, whilst still exhibiting more risk than implemcntation shortfall algorithms.
Note that the aggressivcncss of a POV algorithm may be inferred from its participation rate,
<5% is relatively passive, so this appears to the right of VWAP on the frontier.
Minimalimpact:
Byfocusing solely onminimising the overall marketimpact cost,these algorithms take on
a higher level of timing risk. Consequcntly, they appear on the right hand side of the efficient
trading frontier.
Cost-driven algorithms attempt to balance both cost and risk. Therefore, they will tend to
bc more in the centre of the efficient trading frontier.Although aggrcssive vcrsions will be
closer to the lcft hand side, achieving lower risk, but at a higher expected cost.
ImplementationShortfall(IS):
These algorithms seek to minimize both market impact and risk, oftcn by dctcrmining the
optimalrate of trading.They tend to trademorc quickly thanVWAP or POV algorithms,
resulting in a lower timing risk. Though, this reduced risk is achieved at a slightly higher
expected cost. Thus IS trading algorithms using aggressive (A) or neutral trading styles
appear to the left of POV on the efficient trading frontier shown in Figure 7-10. Only the
passive (P) style exhibits lower cost, although this still has lower timing risk thanVWAP.
Market close(MC):
These algorithms aim to match or better the future closing price.Whercas an

implementation shortfallalgorithm calculates an optimal trade duration,MC algorithms
reverse this proccss to determine an optimal start time. Since their target price is subject to

more volatile and so MC algorithms will often incur higher costs. As a result, they arc
positioned just to the left of implementation shortfall on the efficient frontier,with lower
risk,buthigherexpectedcosts.
AdaptiveShortfall:
An aggressive in-the-money (AIM) adaptive shortfall algorithm hecomes more aggressive
with favourableprices.AsKissell and Malamut (2005b)highlighted this results in a skewed
distribution of returns betwcen rising and falling markets. In comparison, algorithms with a
low sensitivity to price movements (such as POV)have a more symmetrical distribution of

frontier the AIM adaptive shortfall (AS) algorithm will be to the right of the POV algorithm.

Trade horizon
The trade horizon is usually specified by the order's start and end-time parameters. This is
also related to the order size, since we can determine an estimate for the optimal horizon
based on thcADV and the desired tradingrate.
Clearly, a trade horizon that is shorter than the optimal one is more aggressive, although
meeting this requirement can lead to excessive markct impact costs. Whereas, if the horizon
is much longer than optimal then there can be substantial timing risk.For instance, a small

So in terms of algorithm selection, shorter horizons will therefore favour a more
aggressive trading, such as a percent of volume or even an implermentation shortfall
algorithm. Longer horizons favour more passive, impact-driven algorithms, such as an all-

Assetspecificfactors
Asset-specificfactors,suchasliquidity andvolatility,also affect algorithmchoice sincc thy

Liquidity
Liquidity can have a considerable effect on market impact. In fact, it can counteract some ol
the effects of order size, since a large order for a highly liquid asset will tend to cause less
impact than for an illiquid one.Signalling risk can also be an issue for less liquid assets, even
forquitesmall orders.
Since a liquid asset will be easier (and so cost less) to trade than an illiquid one this tends
to widen the potential choice of optimal algorithms.Convcrscly,an illiquid asset limits the
choice to more specialised algorithms, such as liquidity-driven ones.
Volatility
An asset's volatility affects both its expected cost and timing risk. So for volatile assets it is
generally better to select an algorithm that is risk sensitive.In other words, algorithms that
achieve lower timing risk such asimplementation or adaptive shortfall algorithms.

Price trends
A persistent and favourable price trend allows us to reduce costs by trading more passively.
Whilst an unfavourable trend requires more aggressive trading, since any delay will simply
result in even worse executions. Therefore, if we are confident of a price trend persisting
thcn we should consider using algorithms from the appropriate side of the efficient trading
frontierin order to benefit most.For instance, amore passively tradedVWAP algorithm may
perform better for favourable price trends. Alternatively, an implementation shortfall

the level of aggressiveness necds to be appropriate for the size of the expected price trend;
otherwise,the increased market impact costs will counteract anygains/savings.

take advantage of trends.As we have seen these give a more skewcd distribution of expected
costs, with aggressive in-the-money (AIM) strategies achieving a lower cost but higher risk,
whilstpassive in-the-money (PIM)versions do the opposite.If theprice trend is short-lived
Or mean reverts then an aggressive (AIM) approach may be more appropriate.Though, if the
trend persists then the passive in-the-money approach may offer the best results.
So in terms of the efficient trading frontier favourable and persistent trends shift the
selection to the more passive (but riskier) algorithms on the right hand side of Figure 7-10,
whereasunfavourabletrendsshiftittotheleft.

8.1 Introduction
Order placement decisions are a key part of trading. Executing too aggressively could result
in significant market impact; it also broadcasts our intcntions to other market participants.
Whereas trading too passively may result in us failing to complete the order,which could
lead to a sizeable opportunity cost. Therefore we need to find the right balance which best
achievcsourobjcctives.
Based on these requirements, we nced to select each order's size and price, and any
special ordcr types or conditions (if appropriate).Increasingly,marketplaces consist of
muliple competing execution venues.So,for multi-venue markets we also need to choose
the best destination. The possibility of hiddcn liquidity must also be taken into account.
Hencc, order placement decisions are affected by a wide range of factors, such as:
current market conditions (price,volatility and liquidity)
projcctcd future trends
historicalresults
Another way of looking at order placement is in terms of cxecution probability. Factors
such as liquidity and price trends help us to estimate the likelihood of an order executing.
Thcrefore, we can adjust orders to try to maximise their chance of being filled. This provides
a more quantitative basis for actual order selection, and enables us to choose between
execution venues.
To make best use of orders it is vital to understand the actual mechanisms that are
involvcd in order matching.As we sawin Chapter 2,trading consists of three main stages:
1.Price formation
2.Price discovery/trade exccution
3.Reporting,clearing&settlement
Consequently, order placement decisions are closely linked to both price formation and
price discovery(or cxecution).So we shall start this chapter by reviewing these two
fundamental mechanisms in some more detail,beforemoving on to consider the specifics of
order placcment and execution probability.

8.2Price formation
Price formation is a multi-stage proccss. Thc fair value of an asset rcflccts its actual valuc
whercas the market price reflects what people are prepared to pay. Thc markct price may
also reflect their expectations for the future valuc. If dcmand is high and supply is limited,
asscts will often trade at a premium to their fair value. Converscly, if demand is low thcn
discounting may occur.
This divisionis alsoreflected inprice analysis.Fundamcntal analysts tacklc the problcm
by striving to dctermine the fair (or present) value of thc asset.So thc actual markct price
will be the key determinant of whether it is worth trading or not. Converscly,tcchnical
analysts tend to base their pricing solely from trends in the market price and volume.
Givcn the importance of the market price, market transparency also plays a kcy part in
price discovery.A marketmaker's two-way quote onlygives oneview on pricing.Similarly,
if only thebest bid and offcr quotes arc displaycdfrom an order bookthen cffcctivcly this is
the samc as a two-way quote.This adds a degree of uncertainty since tradcrs cannot tell what
other liquidity might bc available. This additional risk could lead to orders being priced more
aggrcssively than is necessary. On the other hand, if quotes are sought from multiple dcalers
or more of the order book is visible then traders can scc thc range of available priccs and
sizes.By using such visible liquidity, they can then adjust their own valuations to detcrmine
theirowntargetpriceforthcasset.
Valuation
The value of an asset is clearly a fundamental component of its price.Many books have been
dedicated to this subject alone. Though, for the purposes of this chaptcr, thc discountcd cash
flow model will sufficc as our pricing model:Present value theory statcs that the prcscnt
value of an asset corresponds to a discountcd sum of its future payments. The discount rate
takes account of the time value of moncy as well as other factors such as risk. Thus, asset
priceswillbehigherforlargcrcashflowsandlowerwhcnthcdiscountrateincreascs.

Inventory-basedmodels
A market maker is not an investor; they are not trying to cstablish a position in a given asset.
Their inventory, or position, simply nceds to be suficient to scrvice any incoming orders. In
order to achicve this, they adjust their quoted prices to encourage orders that take them
closcr to their preferred invcntory size.So the market maker's bid offer spread often tends to
increase as thcir position moves further from their ideal inventory. The strength of this
reaction tends to rcflect their allowed capital; smaller brokers will generally exhibit a more
noticeable effect.
For instancc, Figure 8-1 shows how an example market maker's bid and offer quotes can
change for a rangc of different inventories. The centre of each circle represents their quoted

Information-basedmodels
The value of information was niccly outlined by Hirotaka Inoue (1999) in a study of the
price formation and discovery process: For assets such as governmcnt bonds, where the cash
flowis wellestablished,prices are mainly affected by public information.Macroeconomic
announcements can affect the discount rate, and so alter the present value. Whereas asscts
like stocks are much morc affected by private information, since the futurc cash flows arc
lesscertain.
Information-basedmodels attempt toaccountfor theinformationasymmctrythatis an
important factor in real markets. Some traders will have a definite information advantagc
over others. When trading with such an informed trader we are likely to lose, due to the
resultant price reaction when the information becomes public.This is somctimcs refcrrcd to
as the advcrscselection effect.
AstudybyThomasCopelandandDanGalai(1983)found that toprotcctagainstadverse
selection a market maker's bid offer spread should generate enough returns to cover this
cost. They charactcrised the cost of supplying quotes as writing a put and a call option.
Copeland and Galai concluded that thc bid offer spread is positively related to the pricc and
volatilityandnegativelyrelatcdtomarketactivityanddepth.Theyalsofoundthespreadto
bc ncgatively correlated with the degree of competition faced by market makers.Likewise,
anempiricalstudyofNYSEspecialistsbyCharlcsLce,BclindaMucklowandMarkRcady
(1993) found that they are sensitive to information asymmetry, using both spread and quoted
depth to manage thcir risk.Their study tracked the reactions of specialists to carnings
announcements,afterwhichtheyobserved awideningof thespreads.
Information-based models for order-driven markets are slightly different; this is because
the bid offer spread ariscs duc to market conditions.A wide range of studies has used modcls
oflimit ordermarkets toanalysehow this affccts trading.Apurclyvaluation-based approach
was adopted by Thierry Foucault (1999), using a game theorctic model of price formation for
a dynamic limit ordcr market. Trading occurred due to inherent diffcrences in valuation;
there was no private information.
Foucault's model was extended to incorporate asymmetric information by Puneet Handa,
Robert Schwartz and Ashish Tiwari (2003). Using empirical data from France's main stock
index, the CAC40, they showed that the size of thc sprcad is based on differences in
valuation among the traders as well as the risk of adverse selection. These effects wcre
further quantified in a study by Ming-Chang Wang,Lon-Ping Zu and Chau-Jung Kuo

Trade matching using price/pro-rata based priority is more common in futures markets.
Again,the best priced buy and sell orders take priority,but allocation between orders at the
same price point is donc on a pro-rata basis. That is to say, cach order is allocated based on
ils proportion of the total volume of orders at that price, thus rewarding larger orders.

nearly as much as price.

willnced tobemodified tomanage thisprocess.
Discretionary orders actually have two price limits, a public one and a private one. Just as
iceberg orders hide their true size,discretionary orders hide their true price limit.Thereforc,
when handling discretionary orders the trade matching mechanism needs to also check
whether any orders match on the discretionary price limit.
Contingent ordcrs are more complex bccause they introduce additional dependencies.
They allow links bctween orders,often for different assets.Normally, the order books for
each asset arc completely separale,so conditional orders introducelinkages between them.
Suddenly,the trade matching mcchanismsfor several assetsneed tointeractwith each other
to determine whcther a trade can occur.For this reason,markets that support contingent
orders have tended to handle them in dedicated order books. Hence, spread orders between
futures contracts and some complex optionstrategiesmaybe handled completely separately.
That said, as trade-matching engines become increasingly sophisticated some venues are
now actually starting to use“implied orders”to integrate these complex ordersback into the
main order books. The aim of this is to improve the overall liquidity, although it does add a
considerablelevel of complexityfor thematchingengines.
Researchers are also constantlylookingintoways ofimproving the existing tradc
matching mechanisms. An important area of study is finding a way of balancing the
requircment forvisibility(for price discovery)with the need tohide large orders (toprevent
information leakage).An interesting proposal byPeter Gomber, Miroslav Budimir and Uwe
Schweickert (2006) introduces a new custom order type, the volume order. Essentially, this
is a cross between an iceberg order and a discretionary one: The discretionary price is linked
to a minimum volume requirement, so if there are corresponding orders which can fill this
requircd volume and they are within the price limit then a match may occur. Alternatively,
Leslie Boni and Chris Leach (2004) investigate the“expandable” limit order,which has been
uscd in the inter-dealcr market for U.s. Treasuries. Effectivcly, it gives the trader whose
limit order hadjust executedtheright of firstrefusaltotrade additionalvolume with the
samc dealer. Whilst thcy note that this is useful for trading large block orders, the time taken
for negotiation can he disruptive, since they arc cssentially pushing in front of other orders
on the ordcr book. Boni and Leach propose some potential work-arounds, based on strict
time limitsfor the option to refuse,onlygrantingthisright to thefirst order at a new price
level,or even handling them on a separate order book.Hopefully,morc research will
continue to look into alternative methods for trade matching, since this could well provide
innovative new mechanisms that will help bridge the gap that currently exists between
exchanges and crossingsystems.
Call-basedmatching
A call auction may be carried out as little as once a day, or as frequently as every 10 to 15
minutes throughout the trading day. Rather than continuously matching each order as it
arrives, orders are just queued up and applied to the auction order book. The actual tradc
matching only occurs at the set auction time. So, orders accumulate bcfore the auction takcs
place.This allows longer for price formation and so can help when there is more uncertainty
about what the price should actually be.Consequently,many markets often choose to open

Orderplacementdecisions
Whenmakingdecisionsabout order placementwencedtobalance therequiredobjectives
with the current market conditions.Essentially,we are tryingto find the best price with an
acceptable probability of execution and risk. That used to simply mean choosing a target
price and deciding when and how best to split an order for exccution.
In today's increasingly fragmented marketplaces, choosing where to place an order can be
as important a factor as the price or size.The small average order size now common in many
markets(best typifiedbyequities andlistedfutures)alsomeans thatsignallingriskisnow a
signifieant concern. So to strive for optimal execution we must decide where we are prepared
to trade and how (which order types we will use) as well as how aggressively we will price
andsizeourorder.
Signalling risk
Signalling risk represents the information leakage to other market participants from our
trading strategy.Placing an order on an open order book providcs avaluabletrading option
that other traders may freely execute against. Our trading pattern also relays information to
the other market participants,such as whether we are a large buyer or seller.
Armedwiththisinformation the other participantsmay then adjust their tradingstrategies.
For example,in seeing a large buy order sellers may become less aggressive in their pricing,
since theyknow there is abuycr.Often,it is necessary tohide our actual intentions as much
aspossible,by seekingliquidityfrom alternative sources such as crossingnetworks or“dark
pool"ATSs, or by using special order types.
Note that signalling risk is dependent on both the order size and the asset's liquidity. For
instance,with anilliquidasset evena small order canresult canresultinsignalling risk,
since thcremaybeverylittledisplayedorderbookdepth.Whereasforliquidassets the
increased trade activity and dccper orderhooks means that signallingriskis lesssevere.

8.7 Summary
Price formation is a multi-stagc process. The fair valuc of an assct reflccts its actual
worth whereas themarket price reflccts what people are preparcd to pay.
Markct microstructure rcscarchers have used a wide range of models to invcstigate the
price formationmechanism.Invcntory-basedmodels takc thc dealer's point of view,
whilst informationand order book basedmodelsassume thcre are othcr sourccs of
information,which may in turn affect assct pricing.
Pricc discovcry / trade execution is generally achieved by bilateral trading (with a
market maker) or via auctions (continuous or call-based).

commonly assigned to time (e.g. equitics markets) or pro-rata (size) (e.g. listed

matching.
Mid-point matches may be used for venues that do not have thcir own price discovery
mechanism; here the price is sourced externally, often from the primary exchange.
Order placement dccisions require us to choose where we are prepared to trade and how
(which order typcs we will use) as well as how aggressively we will price and size our
order/s.
In today's increasingly fragmented marketplaces, choosing where to place an order can

9.1
Introduction
Execution tactics represent the micro-level choices that must be made during trading.

trading algorithms and execution tactics is clearest for the earlier schedulc based algorithms.

the next and so on.So for each15-minute period an execution tactic may be tasked with

or offer; alternatively, it could slice the amount into a series of smaller orders, as shown in

trading horizon of seconds orminutesrather than hours.

scll. They may even cancel their ordcrs to see if we are prepared to go even higher.

9.4Summary
Execution tactics focus on the micro level choices that need to be made for the actual
exccution, monitoring the order book and managing order submission. They provide
commonmechanismsto achievethegoals of trading algorithms.
Tactics are often based around existing order types, for instance, pegging and hiding.
For venues that do not natively support these dynamic order types the tactic can adopt an
order placement strategy that essentially mimics the required behaviour. They may also
employmorecomplexlogicthaniscurrently availablevia native order types.
A wide range of common trading mechanisms may be adopted:
Slicingis a straightforwardmeans ofloweringimpact.
Hiding takes advantage of hidden order types or using an opaque ATS.
Layering places orders throughout the book to maximise execution probability and
thepotentialforpriceimprovement.
Peggingprovides dynamic adjustments,adjusting thepriceor even size of orders.
Catching uses a price latch to cut losscs when the market moves away from us.
Sccking actively searches for hidden liquidity.
Sniping takes available liquidity without giving away our own requirements.
Routing determines the best destination for an order based on a range of criteria.
The mainfactors affecting the choice of exccution tactic depend onboth the current
market conditions and how well the algorithm is actually performing.
Trading algorithms may adapt to changing conditions by switching betwcen cxecution
tactics. Alternatively, they may use several tactics in parallel.

Usingvolatilityindices
Volatilityindices provide a measure of themarket expectations for near-termvolatility,often
hasedonthepricesofstockindexoptions.Potentially,wecanalsodecomposevolatilityinto

Thebest-knownvolatilityindexistheCBOE'sVIX,whichwas startedin1993andhas

2003 it was switched to the S&P 500,to be more representative of the U.S.market as a

wide range of puts and calls for the index.It is constantly calculated in real-time; in fact,
futures and options contracts are now available based solely on theVIX.

caters for the NASDAQ 100, and in Europe there are now indices for the DAX, FTSE 100,
