10.4 Handling special events
Computerised trading strategies can react to changing market conditions extremely quickly.
We have already seen how short-tcrm predictions can enable them to make more proactive
dccisions about order placement. Another way of achieving this is to build in rules to
recognise and react to specific market events.For instance,a futures contract has a set expiry
date; we know from empirical evidence that approaching this date much of the trading
volume will switch to the next contraci. Therefore, adjustments may be built in to ensure that
asitreachesmaturity the tradingvolume estimates arerealistic.
These events may be highly predictahle, such as contract expiration, or thcy may bc more
unexpccted,such as a trading interruption due to news.Oftcn they rcsult in sudden rises in
volatility and corresponding drops in liquidity. However, once the cvent has been rccognised
wc can use historical reactions as a guideline, providing short-term predictions for how
market conditions will change, and how long this might last.This should hclp the stratcgy
reactmorelike areal tradermight.
Predictable events
Some events happen at set dates or they are pre-announced, so thcrc is a high degrec of
certainty about them.Thus,it is relatively easy to crcatc custom rules to he applied on these
dates.Good examples of this are:
New bond issues
Futurescontractexpiration
Witching days,when futures and options expire together
Stock index rebalances
In the following sub-scctions, we shall look at empirical examplcs of these cvents and
examinehowtheyaffcctmarket conditions.

Witching days
Witching days occur when several classes of derivatives,for the same undcrlying asset, all
expire on thc same date.This is best typifiedfor stockindices where the expiration of index
futures and options as wcll as equity options is known as“triplc witching". Thc introduction
ofsingle stockfutureshas addedeven morevolume,togethcrwiththemore cumbersomc
monikcr “quadruple witching". The largest witching day is in the U.S., when the quarterly
expirations of S&P 500 derivatives converge.A detailed review of this,and its effects on
trading atbothNYSE andNASDAQ,isprovidcdbyMichaelBarclay,TerrenceHcndershott
and Charles Jones(2006).The volumes involved onwitching days can be huge,forinstance,
in terms of S&P 500 futures alone they note that since latc 2004 between $50-75 billion are
settled on each witching day.
Arbitrageurs account for a sizeablcproportion of thevolume duringwitching days.They
maintainhedgedpositionsinthecashandderivativemarkets,sincethederivativesusually
settle in cash. At cxpiration, they need to closeout thcir cash market positions. To make a
prolit they must target the scttlement price of the derivative contracts. Therefore, on witching
daysthecashmarketsrccciveconsiderableadditionalorderflowfromarbitrageurs.For

IndexRebalancing
Stockindices areimportant benchmarks.In order to accuratelyreflect themarkets they serve
periodic rebalanccs are required. These ensure stocks that now meet the requirements for the
index are added, and those that fail to meet them are removed. Hence, by rebalancing
indices,such as the FTSE 100or the S&P500,manage tokeep representing the major stocks
for theirrespectivemarkets.
Since so many investment firms track the major stock indices any such changes are
publicised well before they actually happen. This gives the investors sufficient warning to
realign their portfolios. To minimize their tracking error, index funds buy stocks added to the
index, and sell those that are removed. So being included in a major index can lead to a
sudden increase in demand for a company's shares.This can lead to a permancnt
improvement initsliquidity,in addition toimprovedcoverageby analysts.Numerous studies
havefound thatstocksthat are addedto anindexsee an abnormalincreaseintheirreturns
whilst the stocks that are removed see a decrease.
A lotofresearchhasfocussed on theS&P500,whichishardlysurprisinggiven thevast
amount of assets that arebenchmarked to this index.*Since1989Standard andPoor'shave
pre-announced adjustments a week in advance. Honghui Chen, Gregory Noronha and Vijay
Singal (2006) analysed the returns for stocks involved in a rebalance, from before the initial
announcement to over twomonths after the index change.Figure 10-18 shows the effect on
the prices of these stocks for the period 1989-2002.
On announcement day, abnormal returns were, on average, +5.12% for additions,
experienced by over 94% of the sample firms. This increased to +8.37% for the day of the

Tradinghalts
Trading halts may be broken down into two main types,those driven by ncws and those that
arisefrom ordcrimbalances.Exchange officialsinstigatenewshaltswheninformation dueto

NYSE supports both types of halts. In their study, Shane Corwin and Marc Lipson (2000)

halts, they also noted that the depth near the quotes falls to unusually low levcls during the
halt,even though specialists and floor traders provide additional liquidity. They also
observed that order flowcould remain atelevated levels for several hours after the halt.
Importantly,thcyfound that the market-clearingprice after the reopeningcall auctionwas a

Price limits
Price limits are gencrally adopted in order-driven markcts. They may be static and/or
dynamic. Static thresholds are usually applied to a benchmark price, such as thc opcn or the
previous close. So a 10% limit from the open restricts the price range betwcen 36 and 44 for
an asset that opened at 40. Dynamic thrcsholds are more versatile and arc often bascd on the
last traded price.For example, a 5% limit on an asset whose last tradcd price was 100 allows
a price range of 95.00-105.00. If the next trade is at 104, the allowed pricc range will shift to
98.8-109.2.
The rules intervene for any trades that would break these ranges and send the market price
either above the high limit or below the low. Such trades may thcn simply not bc permitted,
inwhich casethc tradcr must decidcwhether to alter their pricc or not trade,forcing them to
re-evaluate the market conditions.

For the FIX protocol a lot of this logic is contained within specificFIX engine or gateway

Originally, these galeways were just used by clients to establish a direct connection 10

up their own FIX gateways. Hence, clients now have the possibility of connecting directly to
spccific venues in addition to routing via their broker, as shown by the various pathways
labelled 2 in Figurc 11-5.
To ensure the data quality of messagcs they incorporate both check sums and message

received message matchcs the onc thatwas actually transmitted.

Third-party vendors also offer dedicated algorithmic trading platforms, often bascd on

So there is no point having a super-fast connection to the external data sources, or

Ideally, there should be the minimum number of steps so that data reaches its intended
destination as fast as possible. Data messages should be as small as they can. Though, data
can only be compressed so much. The time they take to be transmitted also depends on the
physical distance they must travel. Table 11-6 shows the results of a round-trip test by
Exponential-e (2009) for their routing service, to give an idea of the time it takes to
communicatebetweendifferentlocations.
Thus, co-location has become inereasingly popular. This allows market participants to
host their computerised trading systems in the same machine rooms as the execution venue,
thus minimising any transmission-rclated delays. Otherwisc, U.S. based brokers will have
considerable latencies when dealing with Asia or Europe,similarly European and Asian
firmswillbedisadvantagedwhenhandlingordersfortheU.S.
It is important to note that latencies will constantly vary, depending on the overall load.At
times when the markets are busicst, or at thcir most volatile,the latencies will inevitably
increase due to the higher workload. Thercfore, is important to track lateney at peak loads
rather than focussing on a minimum figurc, which will have bcen achieved given optimal
conditions.In terms of infrastructure,thingslike careful loadbalancing can help ensure that
processes do not hecome swamped by their workload, introducing additional delays.

Other factors
Speed and capacity are obviously important. However, reliability is also vital. A fast car is
great,unless it breaks down every other day.So the infrastructure also nceds to cope with
every-day usage, as well as handling the loads at peak times. In modcrn markets, this may
mean the infrastructure being available 24x7 (or as close as possible). Therefore,all of the
server-side processeswe sawback inFigure11-6 also need tobe:
·Resilient
·Manageable
·
Sealable
Hardwarc(or software)issues should notresult incatastrophic failure.Therefore,if a
machineorprocessfailsthereshouldbeanothermachine/processreadytoimmediatelytake
over in its placc. This might be achicved by running machines/processes in fault-tolerant
pairs, or using “server farms” to handle processes. Failures should also not be allowed to
propagate,so aproblem with analytics should not disable the algorithmic trading server.
Problems will always occur, so the infrastructure needs to be manageable.Failures should
be simple to spot and correct. Monitoring should highlight the servers/processes that are
under heavier load, since these may be more likely tofail in the future.Load balancing may
also be adopted to try to ensure that the work is distributed evenly amongst the various
processes/machines.
Scalability is another key issue. Obviously,for the long-term it is desirable to be able to
easily extend capacity. There can also be short-term peaks in demand, so a flexible
infrastructure where new servers can easilybe added can be extremely uscful.

Having considered some of the infrastructure surrounding electronic trading let's now take a

requirements aswell as the specificsfor the algorithm.An instance of the algorithmwill then

fundamentallybased on market data.Thus,it needs access to see the available prices and
probably the liquidity. It also needs to be able to create, send and update orders to specific
destinations, which will be one (or several) execution venues. Figure 11-9 shows a simple

Clearingandsettlement
The ultimate goal of any trading platform is to execute trades quickly and efficiently.
Althoughgetting an executionbackfrom an exchangeis onlyhalf the story,sincesettlement
still needsto takeplace.
Electronic trading has led to markedly increased trading volumes,which could have
swamped the clearing and settlement departments.Fortunately,the shift away from manual
trading has helped streamline the process, since most (if not all) of the trade-rclated
information may now be processcd electronically.This has increased thc accuracy and

Just as theFIXProtocol hasproved invaluable as a means oflinking tradingplatforms,it

pre-tradc in their New Order message. Finally, the broker may issue Confirmation
messages that confirm each trade allocation, as well as the fees, account/s and other

importantthatallitscomponentsarewellintegrated.Hence,theappealofcommon
protocols, such as FIX, which providc a uniform messaging structure allowing straight-
through processing(STP) from pre-trade right through to settlement.

12.5 Portfolio trading with algorithms
Conventional trading algorithms may easily be used for trading porufolios, although clearly

targeting a benchmarksuchasVWAPor their arrivalprice.Alternatively,theymight befor

trading algorithms might be specified by the invcstor, or determined by the broker/dealer.
Can“one sizefitall"?
Whcn choosing trading algorithms for portfolios we should first consider whether a single

given by Ian Domowitz and Henry Yegerman (2005a)from ITG. This is based on a large
portfolio transition that was benchmarked using the dailyVWAPfor each asset.The strategy
rcsulted in transaction costs that were approximately double the cstimatc from pre-trade

costs might have been reduced by adopting differing trading strategics,raiher than a“onc
sizefits allapproach.This is illustrated in Figure 12-8.
Tofind a better alternative they classified the orders into thrcemaingroups,based on cach
asset'svolatilityand therelativesizeof theordercomparedtotheaveragedailyvolumc
(ADV).At the two extremes, they found small orders for volatile assets and targe orders for
assetswithamuchlowervolatility.

span multiple days. ln such cases,a more aggressive strategy may be suitable for the first

trading. ln terms of trading algorithms, this might range from a VwAP with a short horizon,
a pcrcent of volumc or a pricc inline.Alternatively, an implementation shortfall or even a
liquidity-bascd algorithm might be used. The choice also depends on other factors such as
investorriskavcrsion,liquidityandpricemomentum.

Cov (I,J)=E((I -μ)(J -v))
where the function EO represents the expected value (or mean), and variables μ and v are

items vary together, so if thc value of I is more than its average then it is likely that J will
also have a higher than normal value. Conversely, a negative covariance means that they
behave in opposite fashions, so a high value for one implies a lower expected value for the
othcr.A covariance of zero shows that the items are completelyindependent, so no inference
maybe madefrom eithervalue.

DeltaHedging
Delta hedgingbalances some of the riskfrom an option position bybuying or selling a set
amount of the underlying asset. This protects against price moves in the underlying.
The value of delta ranges between-1.0 and 1.0.A delta of 1.0 mcans that for every risc
(fall) of $1 in the underlying asset the derivative's price will also rise (fall) by $1.

13.6Arbitragestrategies
Simplc arbitrage,such as assets listing with different prices on multiple venues, is easy to
understand and take advantagc of. Essentially,“we buy low and sell high".Though, all
trading has associated risks: For example, having bought the asset at the first venue, what if
thcmarkctpriceatthcsecondvenuehasadjusted?Suddenly,ourprofitmarginmayhave
disappeared, plus we must also take account of transaction costs. Hence, to try to guarantee
profits any successful arbitrage must minimise risk by incorporatinghedging tcchniques.
As well as simple price arbitrage, each asset class can also have its own particular
arhitragc opportunities. For instancc, yield curve arbitrage takes advantage of discrepancies
in the pricing between short, medium or long-term bonds. Similarly, cash-flow arbitrage

Basis trading
In general, basis trading refers to an arbitrage between a futures contract and its undcrlying
cash product. Though, in thcory it could also be applied to the arbitragc bctwccn othcr
derivatives and thcir corresponding undcrlying assets. The namc is dcrivcd from the concept
of the future's basis (B), which is the diffcrence betwecn the current cash markct pricc (S)
and thc futures contract's price (F):
B=S-F=F=S-B
(13-5)
This is also sometirmcs referred to as the total basis or thc gross basis. Note that when the
gross basis is positive the futurcs price is below the cash price,which is rcfcrred to as normal
backwardation.Alternatively,a negative basis means thefutures price is highcr than thc cash
pricc, sometimcs described as contango.
The basis changes ovcr time, although generally it is lcss volatilc than eithcr thc cash or
the futures prices. Howevcr, towards expiration of the futurc thc two priccs will start to
converge,sincc at expiry thcre isnorealdiffcrcncebetween a futurcs contract and thecash
assct, barring transaction costs. This convergcncc means that the basis must also decrcasc,
and should reach zero when the futures contract expires,as shown in Figure 13-3.

Another way of expressing the relationship between the cash and futurcs prices is the cost
of carry model:
F=S+C
(13-6)
where the cost of carry (C) represents the net costs associated with thc cash position:
Costof carry=Fundingcost+Storagecost--Income earned
In turn, this cost may be represcnted as:
C =(S.rT/365)+A-I
(13-7)

## Page 407

AlgorithmicTrading&DMA
387
where r is funding interest rate, T is number of days until the futures contract expires, A
represents the storage costs and I corresponds to the income earned.
The funding cost is the interest that would have to be paid to fund a cash position for the
pcriod of the futures contract, often this is based on the repo rate. The storage costs and
income earned will diffcr depending on what the underlying asset is. For instance, with
investment assets, such as bonds or stocks, the storage costs will be negligible whilst the
income earned may he considerable (Bonds may earn accrued interest whilst equities may
receive dividends.). Alternatively, for commodities the storagc costs may be sizeable whilst
no income will be generated.
When the net cost of carry is positive thefutures position is more attractive since wewill
not need to make any payments until the future reaches expiry,apart from margin calls.
Whereas if the cost of carry is negative it actually pays to take on the cash position instead.
The net basis, also termed the value basis,adjusts the gross basis for the cost of carry:
Net basis=Grossbasis+Cost ofcarry
Hence,the net basis represents the differcnce betwecn the fair value of thefuture and its
actual market price. A positive value shows it is underpriced, whilst a negative one means it
is overpriced.
Buying the basis means issuing a buy order for the cash asset whilst simultaneously
selling the corresponding futures contract. This is also called cash-and-carry trading. When
we are long the basis, we benefit from any increases in the basis; in other words, from price
riscs for the cash asset or price drops for the future. Effectively, being long the basis allows
us to earn the cost of carry.
Selling the basis is the opposite process,so the cash asset is sold and the future is bought.
This is alsoknown as reverse cash-and-carry trading.A short basis position will benefit from
a decrcasingbasis; cffectively it pays the cost of carry.
These strategicsmay effectivelyheimplemented byusing an appropriate pricingmodel
andlinking the ordersfor thefuture and the underlying asset/s.

Index arbitragc focuscs on the profit opportunities that arise betweenindexfutures and their

although it could also be applied to bond indiccs or even CDS indices.Effectively,it is

Generally, these positions will be closed out once the price discrepancy has disappeared,
rather thanwhen thefuturescontractexpires.
Aswenotcdforthecost ofcarry,theincomeearnedis dependent onthcunderlyingasset.

Transaction costs obviously have a direct impact on arbitrage opportunitics;high costs can

For larger waves, markct impact could be an important factor as well. Also, when shorting

Market regulations can alsohave a noticeable impact on arbitrage.Short sclling
restrictions,such as thcup-tickrule,make itmore difficulttokeep the cash and futurcslegs
synchronized.Market collars also pose a considerable problcm.For cxamplc, thc NYSE
Rule 8OA cnforces a collar based on the DJIA index;whcn triggercd it requires index-
arbitragc orders for the S&P 500 stocks to be stabilizing.So if theindex falls 190 points
(from the prior close) arbitrage orders can onlybe sold on an up-tick;conversely,if it rises
bythis amountbuyordcrsmustbeona down-tick.
To counter some of these issues,arbitragcurs often close out of their positions before the
futures contract expires.Indeed a study of the NYSE by Gcorge Sofianos (1990)found this
to be true for over 70% of positions, with liquidation occurring upon reversal of the original
mispricing or within a few days. Arbitragcurs may also sometimes trade only a portion of the
actual index, instead creating a subset that acts as a proxy. Although this offers reduced
transaction costs, it does create the potential risk of tracking crror between the proxy and the
actual index.
Clearly, successful index arbitrage is non-trivial. Whilst there is still plenty of money to

Option arbitrage
Put-call parity is a key principle in option pricing, most notably dcmonstrated by Hans Stoll
(1969). He highlighted the relationship between thc fair valucs for a pair of identical
European call and put options and their underlying asset, as shown in equation 13-8:
C,+Xe- =P+1
(13-8)
where C is the price of the call option, P is the price of the put, / is the price of the
underlying,X is thcir strike price,ris the interest ratc andtis the time left to expiry.Note
that this depends on theput and the call having the samc strikc price and expiration.
Stoll showed that by using this principle the payoff of any one of the trio may bc recreated
by an appropriatc combination of the other two. Hence, the whole concept of synthetic
option positions was spawned. For example, a synthetic long call is just a long position in the
underlying combincd with purchasing an at-the-money (ATM) put.Altcrnatively,a synthetic
long put corrcsponds to a short position in the underlying togcthcr with thc purchasc of an
ATM call option.
Using put-call paritywe should alwaysbe able to infer the fair price for a call or a put
option based on the prices of the other two assets. So, any mispricing may bc casily spottcd
and taken advantage of by arbitragcurs. If the call option is rclativcly ovcrpriccd thcn a
conversion stratcgy may be used. This means selling the call and hcdging by creating a
synthetic long call position.Alternatively, if the put option is overpriced wc may adopt a
reversal, or reverse conversion stratcgy,which consists of sclling thc overpriccd put and
hedgingwithasynthcticlongput.
A convcrsion strategy comprises of selling ATM call options,and buying the underlying
and ATM puts.Alternatively,we can view this as going long the underlying and creating a
synthetic short position.Figurc 13-4 shows the payouts for this strategy.

13.7Adapting algorithmsformulti-assettrading
In manyways,multi-asset trading algorithms are similar to the two-sidedportfolio trading
algorithms we saw in Chaptcr 12. Though, since they involve a more diverse range of
markets they are more likelyto sufferfrommarked differences inliquidity.This could pose
realproblemsfor achievingbest execution.Therefore,riskmodels need to start expanding to
cope with this.
Factorstoconsiderformulti-assettradingalgorithms
Obviously, the main starting point for any multi-asset trading is to already have successful
algorithms in place for trading cach of the target asset classes.This ensures that any asset
class spccificissueshave alreadybeenidentifiedandappropriate adjustments havebeen
made.
Multi-asset trading adds an extra level of complexity since it will invariably mean trading
across different trading platforms, currencies and time-zones. Hence, it is vital that any
trading algorithms can cope with differences in:
Liquidity
Latency
Transparency
Consistency
Dependency
Otherwise,theremaybe a considerable additional risk exposure.
Liquidity
Aswesawin Chapter3,liquidityvaries considerablybetween thevarious marketsand asset
classes,just as it does between specific assets.Multi-asset trading algorithms need to balance
their trading based on the liquidity of the target assets. Simplistically, this means focussing
on the lowest common denominator, so the most illiquid asset drives the rate of trading.
Forinstance,when tradinga corporate bond against its stock,orders mightonlybeplaced
for the stock leg once an execution has becn confirmed for the less liquid bond.
Alternatively,wc could use legging to provide some more flexibility over execution, just as
we sawfor pairs trades.Though,forvery illiquid assets this could expose us to significant

## Page 418

398
Multi-asset trading
risk.Whilst such approaches will work, they could miss opportunities for the more liquid
assets.
Latency
Lateney can be just as important as liquidity. It makes it harder to rely on the prices we can
see, since by the time our order is handled the price may have shifted.
Each asset elass may well be traded over different platforms, across different execution
venues and possibly even spanning time-zones. Exchanges are now focussed on reaching
turnaround times less than I0 ms.However,there are still plenty ofvenues where this figure
is more like 100 ms or more. So there are bound to be differences in latency bctwcen the
venues.
The actual trading mechanism is another key factor for latency, since it is quite possible
that trading might need to span both order books and request-for-quote (RFQ) or request-for-
stream (RFS) based platforms.In such cases, the difference in latencies might range from
millisecondstoseconds.
For example, let's consider executing a simple pairs trade,both assets have the same
liquidity except one trades at avenue with alateney of50mswhilstfor the otherit is500ms.
If we place a matehing buy and sell order for each asset there is at least 450ms of
uncertainty.A husy trader might not notice thislag;after all,it is equivalent to a fewblinks.
However, it can still have an appreciable effect. In order to compensate for this, the trading
algorithm will have to bias trading towards the venue with higher lateney.
Transparency
Transparency can also vary considerably between markets.Within a single market, differing
levels of transparency have proved fairly successful.Highly transparent primary venues
allow for casy price discovery,whilst more opaque venues enable volume discovery.Indeed,
the “dark pool"” ATSs have proven so successful for equities because although being opaque
their price discovery tends to be based on the primary exchanges.
Across asset classes, differences in transparency can pose more of a problem, since there
are no equivalent links.For instance, the entire order book might be visible when trading
stocks,but for other assets we might only he able to see the hest bid and offer.Although wc
might have confidence of best executionfor our stock trading,it is much harder tohave this
fortheotherassets.
Consistency
Consistency is another major factor for ensuring successful multi-asset trading, particularly
for transaction costs. As we saw in section 13.6, there is a wide range of arbitrage
opportunities between asset classes.For these to be profitable it is vital that any additional
costs are considered when looking at relative prices.This might be as obvious as
incorporating the different bid offer spreads,commissions or routing/handling fees.
However, it must also include asset specific factors such as storage/delivery fees, accrued
interestordividendpayments.
Dependency
Over the years,microstrueture studies have analysed the price relationships across many of
the differcnt asset classes.For example, studies have focussed on whether the futures
markets lead or lag the markets for their underlying assets. Such inter-market relationships
are animportant source ofinformationforshort-termpredictions ofprices and othermarket

## Page 419

conditions, as we will see in Chaptcr 15. Taking advantage of these could be the differcnce
bctwcen a profitable trading strategy and a loss-making one.
Minimising risk
Lower transaction costs may bc achieved for portfolios by maximising the natural hedging,
or divcrsification, for as long as possible. Therefore, it is quite likely that risk-based models,
similar to thosewesawforportfoliotrading,willbe atthehcart of nextgenerationmulti-
assct algorithms. Clearly,constructing multi-asset risk modcls is more complex than the

Multi-asset trading strategies are now morc widcly accessible due to electronic trading:

Liquidity
Latency

News mining
News mining combincs the analysis of historical data with informationfrom ncws archives.
At present,much of the research focuses on interpreting the text from newsheadlines/storics

markct impact of ncws. Artificial intelligence (Al) techniques, such as neural networks or

As we sawin theprevious sub-sections,accuratelyinterprcting the meaningof newsis a
complex task.Many studies struggle to achicve better than 50% accuracy.Though,given
time,it is likely that scmantic analysis will improve sufficicntly to make such tcchniques a

availableinmachine-readableformatssuchasXML.
Analysing thc short-term impact ofnews is an easiergoal than cstimatingits mid and
long-tcrm effects. By comparing the news data, such as EPS figures, with market
expcctations we can determine how much of a surprise the ncws actually is. If the news
meets expectations thenthemarketwillmostlikelyalready havc incorporatedthis
informationinto the asset'sprice,so a significantprice changeis unlikely.Whereas if the
news is a huge surprise then a period of volatility will be likely, whilst the market adjusts to
this ncw information. Section 14.5 provides a review of empirical market studies detailing
theseshort-termeffects.

News announcements represcnt a flow of information to the markets. Sincc most asset priccs
arebascd on such information it is hardly surprising that news can have a markcd clfect.
A large number of empirical studies have analysed the impact of news for most of the
major markets.In this section,we will review thcse to see thc cffects ofboth macrocconomic
and corporate news on prices, trading volumes, liquidity and volatility. We shall also
consider how other factors,such as the business cycle,affect the markct rcsponse to news.
Reactionstomacroeconomicnews
Macrocconomic news gives a regular indication of the performance of an cconomy. The
announcemcnts maybe used to predict future economic growth,so thcy can have a markcd
ellect on thc trading of most asset classes. For instancc, if key indicators show signs of a
recession then governments may be prompted to change interest racs or altcr thcir fiscal
policy. Companies may well have to adjust their expccted earnings in the light of thcse new
conditions. Likewise, investors may choose to alter their portfolios, shilting to safer larger
capstocksorincreasingtheproportionofbonds.
The impact of news on asset prices varies somewhat for dilferent assct classcs. For
example,news of anintercstratedropwill helpincreasethe price of existingbonds,whilst it
weakens the currency. For corporations, the picture is slightly more complex, sincc thcy may

Reactions tocorporate news/announcements
Corporatc news is obviously much more closely linked to specific assets than

Tetlock, Maytal Saar-Tscchansky and Sofus Macskassy (2008) found that company news
tended tocluster aroundearnings announcements.

One of the factors that make corporate announcements different from macroeconomic
news isthattheexact dates of thesenotices canvary considerably.Estimatesfortheseused
to be from calendar-based calculations, although it is becoming more common for firms to
provide the expected dates for their next announccment. Products such as Thomson
Financial's First Call Corporation nowprovide centralisedsources for these dates.Other
than providing a warning forupcoming announcements,the estimated dates may actually bc
used tohelppredictwhether thenewswillbegoodorbad.Thisisbecausefirms tendtobe
kcen to announce good news and deferissuingbad news.A more quantitative analysis of this
cffect was performed by Mark Bagnoli, William Kross and Susan Watts (2004). They
analysedthereturnsforU.S.stocksbasedonthelagbetweenthcestimateddatesand the
actual corporate announcements,for around 26,000 examples between 1995-8.They found

14.6Incorporatingnewsintotradingstrategies
Precognition, or “second sight",would clearly be a very useful add-on for most invcstment
and trading strategies.Howcvcr,the focus of this book is on execution,not investmcnt.
Though we may not bc ablc to reliably predict exactly what information news will bring, we
can still cstimatc how the market might react, as we sawin the prcvious section.Thesc short-
term predictions of market conditions may enable our trading strategics to take advantage of
the market response, rathcr than simply reacting to the rapidly changing conditions.
Even though we are using news to augment trading strategics, rathcr than to gcneratc
invcstment ideas, certain precautions are still necessary. Corrcct interprctation is vital
otherwise, the estimates for the market response will be wrong. The accuracy and validity of
informationisalsoimportant.
An easy way of incorporating news into trading stratcgies is to usc indicators. They
providc a simple means for algorithms to interpret whether news is good or bad,and so
respond accordingly.These may then be added to adaptive trading algorithms alongside thc
price trend and short-term liquidity indicators that many already usc.In thc future,we might
alsostart toscemoreopportunistienews-driven algorithms.

Importantprecautionsfordatamining
Statistical analysis is an important tool, but it can also be a dangerous one.Indeed, there arc
lics, damned lies, and statistics, as popularised by Mark Twain (1907).As with any analysis,
due care must be taken to check any potcntial relationships which may be discovered. It is
essential to apply economic sanity chccks and awide range of testingbefore toomuch is
readinto anyrelationship.
Stefan Zemke (2002) provides a nice review of some of the potential pitfalls that should
be consideredwhen handling financial data.Inparticular,he emphasises theimportance of
the data prc-proccssing.To start with,we must be sure that the data quality is good cnough.
The old maxim “garbage in,garbage out” holds just as true for statistical analysis as for
computcr programs. Therefore,it is important to have checks in place to inspect and, if
necessary, clean the data. Apparent outliers may in fact be genuine; thcy may bc due to
events such as stock splits or dividends.Similarly,missing data mayneed tobe back-filled,
orsimplyexcluded.
Inferring relationships from data must also be done with some caution.Again,it is
important to remcmber that any associations often simply reflect a probability, rather than a
truly causal relationship: Just because one event has happened, it does not necessarily
guarantee anything-althoughit may makerelated eventsmorelikely to occur.A commonly
cited example is thc “Texas sharpshooter” fallacy: If we just look at a targct with several
shots in the dead centre,we might assume that the shooter had agood aim.Howevcr,without
havingscen thcshotswe donotknowhowfar theyweretakenfrom,orevenwhether thc
targctwaspainted on afterwards!In other words,itis always important to checkwhether thc
discovered relationships make cconomic sense.This may also mean taking into account
factorssuch astransaction costs.
For relationships to be meaningful, they must be based on a reasonably sized dataset. Two
points can always be joined by a straight linc (with an R? of 1.0 or 100%). For instance, hack
inFigure15-1we saw that the dataforU.S.lemon imports andpedestrianfatalitieswere
very closely related,with an R² of 0.93.However, this is only for annual results from 1994-
2000; in fact, this range was chosen solely because it happened to give a high correlation and

workshop on computers and intelligencc at Dartmouth. AI systcms are designed to adapt and
learn,andsocffectivelythinkfor themsclves.
Thc progress of Al has certainly had its fair share of“ups and downs”.Buoyed by carly

Types of artificial intelligence
AI can actuallybesplit intotwomain approaches:
Convcntional AI
·Computationalintclligence
Conventional AI is a top-down approach that uses logic and rules to make decisions. This
generally relies on data that has been translated into known symbols, employing custom-
madcknowlcdge bases or statistical analysis.Examples of conventional AI include expert
and case-based reasoning systems, as wcll as Bayesian networks.
On the other hand, computational intelligence is a bottom-up approach that takes its
inspirationfrombiologicalmechanisms.Forinstance,neuralnetworks try torcproducc thc
action of ourbrain's neurons,whilst evolutionary computation simulatcs populations.Othcr
examples are hybrid intelligent systcms,which are a combination of neural and evolutionary
mcchanisms,whilstfuzzy logicoffcrsprobabilitybased solutions.
ConventionalAl
Convcntional AI is gcnerally based on logic. Experts define rulcs for how to identify specific
situations and what actions to take in response to them. These may be broken down into
simple logical statemcnts: IF <this happens> THEN <do this> ELSE <do this instcad>.
Rules also need to be placed in contcxt; hence, structures like decision trccs may be used to
ensure they arcfollowcd in a sensible order. Once cnough of these are defined, a system has
all the basics of how to cope. Obviously, though, there are some subtle nuances - thcre will
alwaysbcsituations that simplydonot follow therules.
Allof this sounds rather familiar, since a trading algorithm is essentially a complex
collection of rules each designcd to rcspond to various events. The rules themsclves have
generally becn detcrmincd by experienced traders or quants. So, in essence, a trading
algorithmis just aninstanceof anAI expert systcm.
Conventional AImay be also used to makeforecasts;however,the reliance on explicit
rulesmcansitislessadaptablethantechniqucsinvolvingcomputationalintelligence.
Computationalintelligence
Computational intelligence, or soft computing,applies an array of different techniques,using

Optimisation is also important. For many problcms, therc is an optimal solution, which

Likewisc, adaptation is another key consideration. One of the downfalls of conventional

15.4 Incorporating in trading strategies
Trading algorithms and execution tactics can adapt to market conditions.Limit ordermodels
may be used to determine the execution probability of orders, whilst cost-models help
estimate the potential market impact and risk associated with a trading strategy. Hence, it is
not a great leap to consider adding short-term forecast models. These may also be used to
augmentmodelsforexccutionprobabilityand/orcostestimates.
Algorithms may be broken down into specific trading rules. Generally, these are defined
by experienced traders, or quants,based on expcrience of what works best for a specific
market. Often this rcquires a substantial amount of testing and fine-tuning. Artificial
intelligence systems offer a way of enhancing this process, since they can dynamically test a
huge numbcr of variations in parallel. Evolutionary algorithms may be used to fine tune
trading rules and/or their parameters. Alternatively, whole rulc-sets or algorithms could be
evolved.Closely linked with this,is the ability to back-test the rules or strategies to
determine their performance.By successfully automating both of these processes,we should
be able to harness the power modern computers provide to literally test thousands of
combinations.

trading algorithms.However,during the execution it is important to remember that we do not
know exactly what the future holds. So from time T in Figure 15-13 all we really have is
uncertainty.

The techniques we have covered in this chapter may seem somewhat esoteric. Still, if AI
systems can be used to drive a car 60 miles through town and park it without crashing, then
there is certainly some scope for them to be applied to the financial markets. It is important
to remcmber that we are not talking about recreating human intelligence. Best execution
seems like a fuzzy goal,but it is still less complicatcd than life.AI systems for trading are
not conscious and they cannot communicate.In terms of raw intelligence, the goal is
probably more like that of an insect,which (in theory) should be a lot more achievable.
That said, the financial markets have thousands of traders,eachwith their own opinions
and stratcgies.Collectively their behaviour shapes the markets,and so affects the prices of
assets. Advances are certainly being made in collectivc intclligence, using massive multi-
agent simulations. But this an incredibly complex phenomenon, so the science of forecasting
markct reactions is still evolving.

Starting in 1963, the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) recommended
restructuring overthe counter(OTC) trading,leadingto thecreation ofNASDAQ.Whilst
the NationalMarket System(NMS)was introducedto consolidate price andtrade
information amongst the various exchanges, as well as provide an inter-market system (ITS)
to route orders between them.Thcn in 1997,NASDAQ ordcr handling rules were introduced
to offerinvestors more protection for thcir limit orders,and to ensure that dealcrs always
displayed their best quotes. The ruling to display client limit orders (when priced bctter than
the dcaler's quote)helped push NASDAQ away from being a purely quote-driven market to
incorporating bchaviourmorelike a limit orderbook.Notably,though,it was the quote
ruling which had the most impact.Prcviously,dcalcrs had bcen able to use private inter-
dealcr systcms to trade at better priccs;the ncw ruling meant that these priccs should also bc
availableto thepublic.In effect,this opened awindowonNASDAQfor external cxccution
venues,and suddenly many newECNs were created,all competingfor market sharc.

Decimalisation was introduced in 2001,leading to lower bid offer spreads. The resultant
0.1 cent tick size also encouraged the practice of“pennying”(jumping ahead of an existing
order simply by upping the price by a penny). Decimalisation has helped continue the trend
of smaller order sizes and so has encouragcd traders with large orders to use alternative
venues, in particular the newer ATSs or so-called “dark pools". Last, but not least,
RegulationNMSwasimplementedin2007,providingrulesfor:
Fair access
Order protection
Aholishing sub-pcnny pricing
Marketdatarevenueallocation
In part, these rekindle the earlier 1975 regulations, although they meant scrapping the ITS.
Instead,thefairaccessrulemandates thatprivatelinksmustbeestablishedto allowvenucs
to route orders between each other. In addition, venues capturing a significant proportion of
the ADV must provide a market quote. The order protection (or “trade-through") rule
requires that trades must be executed at thebest displayed price accessible inunder a second.
So an order placed on theNYSE will actuallybe routed andexecutedwherever the best
quoted price is, be it NASDAQ or an ECN. In comparison, the ITS allowed a 30 second time
window for an order to be acted on, whilst this may have seemed reasonable 30 years ago,in
a market where trading is now often measured in milliseconds this delay is a lifetime. In fact,
this huge delay put the ITS order creator at a considerable disadvantage to the market, as
Larry Tabb points out in an article for the TABB Group (2003). Regulation NMS should
help increase market competition,but its long-term impact remains to bc secn.
The 2007-09 financial crisis also triggered a fresh look at many aspects of the U.S.
marketplaceby regulators.Initially,the focus was on short selling,but has since expandcd to
look at the “dark pool” ATSs and the use of IOIs, as well as “flash" orders and high-
frequency trading.Only timewill tellwhat newregulations result andhow they affcct the
markets.

Continuous crossing systcms havc grabbed a significant proportion of the market share.A

Continuous blind crossing systcms have also bccome increasingly popular. In 2001, the

exchangc,ECN or possibly even another ATS.Similar approaches are offered by Instinet's

Advertised crossingis another important mechanism,for whichPipeline is probably the

Lifcwould be a lot simpler,and more efficient,if therewerea single depository like the
U.S. Dcpository Trust & Clearing Corp. (DTCC). The choice of depository can also affect
the trade cost since each may have different settlement costs. Therefore, liquidity
aggregation is only really appropriate for prices from venues that share the same depository,
as noted in a white paper on market data consolidation from Instinet (2007). Otherwise,
additional costs may be incurred which are not reflected in the price. Cross-border settlement
has traditionallybeen expensiveinEurope.
A rcport by thc Deutsche Borse Group (DBG/Clearstream) (2002) noted that wholesale
tradcs could be 30% more expensive, whilst retail ones were up to 150% more. Thus, until
there is further consolidation amongstEurope's depositories, smart order routing systems
and trading algorithms will need to take these additional costs into account. Fortunately,
there arc somc signs that this situation should improve.A subsidiary of the U.S. DTCC has
launchedEuroCCP,which provides a unifiedclearing and settlement facility that is used by
Turquoise.

Assetspecific
Forcign cxchangc represcnts thc trading of currencics, essentially by the transfcr of

What we first think of as foreign exchange is spot trading.This corrcsponds to a cash

availability of forwards allows both counterparties to hedgc against shifts in thc cxchange
rate; conversely,speculators will try to predict and bcnefit from thcm.An FX option is
similar, although it gives the purchaser the right to buy or sell, rather than an obligation.
Forcign exchangc swaps consist of two legs,a standard spot FX transaction linked with a
simultaneous FX forward trade.Initially,the two currcncies are exchangcd,and when thc
outright matures, they are swapped back again, at thc pre-agreed ratc. A currency swap is
slightly different since it represents an exchange of intcrcst payments for undcrlying fixcd

FX tradingis largely conccntrated on a small subset of currcncics.Infact,aroundtwo thirds

Pricing foreign cxchange rates can be quite difficult, since they are affected by a wide
range of cconomic factors. Traditional exchange rate determination models based solely on
macroeconomic factors have failcd to explain and forecastfluctuations in exchange rates.
This has been clearly noted in studies by Yin-Wong Cheung, Menzie Chinn, and Antonio
Garcia-Pascual,(2005)and Richard Meese and Kenneth Rogoff (1983).An alternativc
method of pricing is to adopt a market microstructure-based approach. This has heen
pioncered by Martin Evans and Richard Lyons (2002),and Lyons (2001). In thcse models,
macroeconomic information affects exchange rates directly,but also indirectly via order
flow, or net buying pressure. Subsequcnt studies have shown that order flow can both
explain and forccast changes in exchange rates.For more information, see the work by
Dagfinn Rimc, Lucio Sarno and Elvira Sojli (2008) and Evans and Lyons (2005).
Both exchange rates and order flows react to macroeconomicfactors such as changes in
economicgrowth,inflation,interestrates orbudget/tradebalances.Anysuchinformation,
whichmight reflect futurc ordcr flows,canhave an important,and oftenimmediate,effect
on exchangc rates.This can make the tradingvolumes quite volatile.Indeed,the spot markct
canvarybyup to30%day today,as noted byNaureenMalikfrom theWall Street Journal
(WSJ)(2004).Whilst the actual news is publicly broadcast,global order flow is still
rclativcly opaque. Clearly,the majorbanks have an advantage here since the more clients
theyhavethen themoreorderflowinformation theypossess.
Anothcr factor,which can have a considerable effect onforeign exchange,is the
possibility of ccntral bank interventions. Although these may be able to smooth short-term
fluctuations, it is just no longer feasible to prop up a currency for any length of time. For
instance,the infamous Black Wednesday (16° September 1992) when the U.K.finally
announced it was withdrawing from the European exchange rate mechanism. This netted
ovcr a billion dollars profit for speculators,who had shorted up to $10 billion inpounds
sterling in the previous two weeks, anticipating of the pound's fall from grace. Central bank
intervcntion is also an intcresting signal for investors, since it can indicate future changes in
monctary policy.

Swapsmarkets
Swaps are one of the most important types of dcrivativc, accounting for around half the
global outstanding notional value in the first half of 2008, as we saw back in Table E-1.
Essentially, a swap is an agreement between two counterpartics to exchange cash strcams.
These streams may bc linkcd to fixed/floating interest rates, currencies, or evcn dividend
paymcnts. Thus, they offer a flexible means of controlling cash flows, which gocs some of
thewaytocxplainingtheirpopularity.
SwapsarestillessentiallyviewcdasanOTCderivativc.Though,thcshccrvolumeof
intcrest rate swaps mcans there can be considerable liquidity for thc morc standardiscd
contracts.Hence,electronic tradingis bccoming more important.
Assetspecific
A swap contract is a bilatcral agrccment to exchange cash strcams for a principal amount
over a set time period. Generally, thc associated cash streams are bascd on intcrcst ratcs or
currencies(orboth),althoughtheycan alsoincorporatcflowsfromcquiticsorcommoditics.
For cxample,a cashstreammightcorrespond to theincome orintercstpaymcntsfrom a
specific bond, the interest rate of a spccific fixing (such as LIBOR) or thc gains/losscs from
marking to market a stockposition.As with bonds,swaps may bc classified by thc maturity
date: short-term range from a week to less than 1-2 years, mcdium tcrm rangc from 1-10
years whilst long term may last up to 50 years. Swaps give organisations an cxtrcmcly
flexible means of controlling thcir cash streams, although their individuality also means they
havc primarily been traded OTC.
The commoncst typc is an Interest Rate Swap (IRS).Note that the principal (or notional)
amount is not actually exchanged; only the associated interest payments arc swapped. A
vanilla interest rate swap consists of one lcg bascd on a floating rate of interest whilst the
other is based on a fixed rate. For the floating leg, the actual paymcnts are determined by the
fixing schcdulcs for the interest rate, e.g. quarterly for the thrcc-month London Interbank
Overnight Rate (LIBOR), whilst the fixed leg is usually paid semi-annually. Altcrnatively, a
basis swap is one where both legs are based on floating rates, albeit with differcnt fixing
sources or schcdules.
As its name suggests, a currency swap adds exchange rates into thc mix. Howcvcr, it also
requires cxchange of thenotional amount atmaturity andoptionally atthcstartof the
contract. This allows companics to borrow in the currency where thcy can obtain thc bcst
interest rate then convert it to the currcncy they actually need. The most common typc of
currency swap involves a floating U.S. dollar rate (often based on LIBOR)with a fixcd rate
in anothcr foreign currcncy.Note that a currency swap should not be confusedwith a forcx
swap,which justrepresents an exchange of currencies.A forex swapis the combination of a
spotFX transaction together with a forward contractto reverse this initial exchangc and so
close out thc dcal;interest paymcnts are notinvolved.Effectively,aforexswapreprcsents a
spreadtradehetwecnthespotFXrateandtheforwardrate.
An ovcrnight indexed swap (OIS) is similar to a vanilla IRS,with aleg linkcd to an
overnightfixing.Atmaturity,thedifferenccbetwccnthcaccruedintcrcstforthefixedrate
and the averagc of thc floating rates is exchanged. These are usually short-tcrm swaps with
maturitiesrangingfromaweektotwoycars.
A total return swap exchanges periodic intercst payments for the total return of an assct or
basket of asscts.This allows investors acccss to capital gains,without having to actually hold
the assct/s, since the ownership is not transferred. Effectively, they providc thc purchascr

Assetspecific
Credit derivativcs act as financial guarantees that may be used to provide protcction against a

A credit default swap(CDS)is a contract in which the credit riskfor a notional amount of
debt issued from one (or more) cntities is transferred. The purchaser gains protection from
thiscredit risk,whilst the seller is paid regularprcmiums for the lifetime of the contract.If a

CDSindicesrepresentanaturalevolutionfromsingleentityor basketCDSs.These

Depositaryreceipts
Depositary reccipts allow trading in sharcs of forcign companies without having to carry out
any cross-border transactions.Note that these are for single companies and bear no rclation

Asset specific
Depositary receipts (DRs) essentially act as proxies for foreign shares that may bc tradcd
locally eithcr at exchanges, other exccution venues or OTC. They are issued by a domcstic
bank or brokerage against thcir own invcntory of the forcign stock. Note that the ratio of
shares does not havc to be 1:1,so a single depositary rcceipt might translatc to 0.5,5,10 or
even 100 foreign shares, depending on the share pricc. A sponsored DR mcans that thc
depositary bank is also involved with the forcign company,for instancc, organising proxy
votes for the DR holders. An un-sponsorcd DR is issued without such involvcment, so
holders may not receive the same shareholdcr benefits or voting rights. Any dividends are
gencrallypaid in thc local currcncy,and for afce the depositary bank will convert the
reccipts back into the underlying stock. So in many rcspccts they behave rmuch likc domcstic
stocks.

Pricing and trading
A depositary reccipt is based on an underlying asset, namely a forcign stock. Its value is
dcpcndcnt on the current market pricc of this underlying asset,rather than some future value.
Thcrefore,the price of a DR should he similar to theprice of the forcign stock,adjusted by
the currcnt markct exchange rates. Note that the conversion ratio is usually chosen by the
depositary agcnt to best reflect the value of the foreign shares. Hence, the price of most
ADRs is between $10 and $100.So for cheaper stocks cach ADR share might equate to
hundreds of actual shares in the company.
There are some complications, though: A true price comparison should also factor in the
fccs associated with convcrting a DR into the actual stock. The savings in managcment and
settlcment costswhich theDRoffcrsmay alsobe reflected in theprice of theDR.Alsothere
is the transaction cost associatedwith anyFX trades to consider.So differences in the prices
of the twoassctsdonot necessarilyrepresent arbitrage opportunities.

ExchangeTradedFunds
Investment funds are collectivc investment schemes.Howcver,thcy can also be tradcd as
asscts.Funds may be categorised as cither open-ended or closcd-cndcd.This relatcs to their
size; open-cnded funds can continuously cxpand or rcduce, whcreas closcd-ended funds
maintain a fixed size.
Perhaps one of thc best-known typcs of open-ended fund is thcU.S.mutual fund.For ncw
investors the fund manager must issue additional shares,whilst for dcparting invcstors thcy
must redeem them for cash or securities. Historically, open-ended funds were hought or sold
based on the day'scloscprices.
Closed-ended funds (CEFs)behavc more like stocks.Therc is an initial distrihution of a
fixed number of sharcs in the fund,much like an IPO. Subscquently,invcstors wanting to
joinor leavc thefund will gencrally necd to trade the shares on thesccondary markcts.
The exchange-traded fund (ETF) was first introduced in the early 1990s. Initially, thcse
werc simply open-ended funds which were tradable intraday on the sccondary markct, just
like closed-ended funds.Exchangc traded funds are becoming anincrcasinglypopular way
for fund managers to gain an ovcrall market exposure, or to provide hcdgcs for risk
management.Infact,theyhave provcn tobe so successful that a rangc of closed-cnded funds
now alsoclass themselves asETFs.
Asset specific
ETFs are generally classified as either being index or optimiscd funds.Indcxfunds passively
track or replicate a specific bcnchmark,whilst optimised funds try to hcat market
henchmarks and so adopt similar techniques to aetiveinvestors.
Initially, most open-ended ETFs concentratcd on major stock indices as their bcnchmarks.
Nowadays, scctor specific ETFs are becoming commonplace, as are ETFs containing foreign
assets. They are not just restricted to equities; ETFs may also be creatcd bascd on portfolios
of bonds or evcn commodity futures. Fixcd income ETFs are useful bccause the fund
managerisresponsiblc for maintaining the portfolio, so bonds arcrolled bcforc they mature
and coupon payments are reinvested. Likewise, for commodity ETFs thc managcr handles
the margin requirements and again rolls any contracts heforc expiry.
Optimised ETFs often track custombenchmarks,which are createdby applying strict
rules and quantitative techniqucs. This allows thcm to prcscrvc their transparcncy.ETFs
have even heen creatcd to cater for specificinvcstmcnt styles.For instancc,the Claymore
MacroShares Oil Down fund compriscs of assets that will benefit from a drop in oil prices,
whilst their Insider ETF invests in 100 stocks in which insiders havc recently heen buying.
ETFs offer several advantages to othcr typcs of investmcnt funds:
·Transparency
·Lowcrfecs/overall cost
·Tax cfliciency
In gencral,ETFs employ fixed compositions,often publishcd daily, so they arc morc
transparent than other typcs of funds. In comparison, for some activcly managcd mutual
funds or closcd-cnded funds the publicly availahlc compositions mayhe months old,in part
to protcct thcir investments. ETFs also tend to have lower fccs, particularly for the more
straightlorward indcx trackers.For instance,thc SPDR ETF,which covcrs the S&P 500
index,has an cxpcnse ratio of 9.45 bps, whilst many mutual funds quotc an cquivalcnt cost
around doublc this.Meanwhilc active funds may chargc anywhcrc from 100-150 bps or

Pricingandtrading
Thc nct assct value (NAV)of a fund is simply the total valuc of all the asscts in the fund
dividcdbythcnumbcrofsharesissued.Foranopen-cndcdfundtheNAVrepresentsthe

Arbitragccnsurcs thatthcmarketvalue of theETFkeepsinlinewiththeNAV,sinceif
the ETF tradcs at a premium (discount) the dealers will just sell (buy) thc ETF and buy (scll)
thc undcrlying assets. In comparison, closcd-cnd funds may trade at a considerable premium
ordiscounttothcirNAV,basedonanalysts/tradersestimatesfortheactualvalueoftheir

ETFs may bc freelybought and sold on thc sccondary markets throughout the trading day.

## Page 595

AlgorithmicTrading&DMA
Advancedexecutiontechniques,such asalgorithmictrading,have
alreadyprovedtheirvalue,insomeofthemostvolatilemarkets.
Toget thebestout of these toolsit isvital to understand themfully.
Thisbookprovidesa thoroughgrounding,helpingyouget up to
speedonthesestrategiesandhowbesttousethem.
Electronic tradinghas transformed the markets.Algorithmic trading andDirect Market Access(DMA)are
important tools helpingbothbuy and sell-side traders to achieve best execution.
Thisbookstartsfrom thegroundup,providingdetailed explanations ofboth these techniques:
Anintroductiontothedifferenttypesofexecutionisfollowed byasummaryofmarketmicrostructure theory.
Throughout thebookexamplesfromempiricalstudiesbridge thegapbetweenthetheoryandpracticeof trading.
Ordersarethfdamentaluildinglocksoranyxeuin stragy.Marktmitsophidenrg,
routed and immediate-or-cancel orders are all described,using illustratedexamples.
Tradingalgorithms are explained,andcomparedusingcharts to showpotential tradingpatterns.TWAP,VWAP
PercentofVolumeMinimal mpactImplementationShorfallAdaptiveShortfallMarketOnCloseandPairs
trading algorithms are all covered,togetherwith commonvariations.
Transactioncosts can have a significanteffect oninvestment returns.Anin-depth example shows how thesemay
bebroken downintoconstituentssuch asmarketimpact,timingrisk,spread andopportunity costandotherfees.
Coverage includesall themajorasset classes,from equitiestofixedincome,foreignexchange andderivatives.
Detailed overviewsforeach of theworld'smajormarkets are providedin the appendices.
Order placement and execution tactics are covered in more detail,aswell as potential enhancements(such as
short-term forecasts),for thoseinterested in the specifics of implementing these strategies.
Cuttingedgeapplicationssuchasorfolioandmult-asset tradingarealsoconsideredasarehandlingnew and
datamining/artificial intelligence.
